title: Identification automatique de domaines de connaissances dans un dictionnaire universel du XVIIIe s.
abstract: On se propose de présenter les résultats d’une recherche visant à l’identification et à la classification automatique de domaines de connaissances dans un dictionnaire universel du XVIIIe siècle.L’œuvre support des analyses est l’édition de 1743 du Dictionnaire Universel François & Latin (désormais, DUFLT) dit de Trévoux. Environ 20 % des articles héberge un ou plusieurs paragraphes associés à une marque de domaine (Pétrequin 2009, Turcan 2024) qui stipule de quelle science (astronomie ...), art (poësie ... forge...) ou métier (charron ...) relève le contenu. On est loin de la systématicité de l’Encyclopédie de Diderot et d’Alembert (1751-1772) où 83% environ des articles est pourvu d’une marque de domaine (données tirées de l’ARTFL et de l’ENCCRE). Notre objectif est de parvenir à une classification complète de l’ensemble des paragraphes du dictionnaire en leur affectant un ou plusieurs domaines de connaissance. Pour ce faire, nous développons une approche combinant grands modèles de langage (LLMs) et modèles de classification supervisée. On soulignera que la classification en domaines de connaissances a déjà fait l’objet de plusieurs études computationnelles sur l’Encyclopédie de Diderot & d’Alembert (Horton et al. 2009, Roe et al. 2016, Brenon et al. 2022), mais qu’aucune n’a été conduite à ce jour sur le DUFLT.Dans une première partie, nous présenterons les choix méthodologiques qui structurent notre démarche. Nous justifierons le choix du paragraphe comme unité de base de nos analyses, le regroupement des marques de domaine (simples : en termes de géographie ...; complexes : Terme de Botanique & de Pharmacie) en un nombre restreint de « macro-domaines ». Nous aborderons également les difficultés liées à l’hétérogénéité de ces marques et à la nature parfois pluri-/inter-disciplinaire de leurs contenus.Dans une seconde partie, nous décrirons le protocole expérimental mis en œuvre. À partir d’un ensemble de paragraphes initialement pourvus d’une ou plusieurs marques de domaine (que l’on aura retirées), nous sollicitons différents LLMs dans un cadre de classification few-shot afin de leur faire associer un ou plusieurs macro-domaines. Les prédictions sont ensuite évaluées par comparaison avec les annotations existantes. Cette phase permet d’identifier les configurations de prompts et les modèles les plus performants, et d’affiner progressivement les instructions fournies aux modèles. Les résultats préliminaires montrent qu’un des modèles testés (Gemini 3.5 Flash) atteint un F-score proche de 70 % sur un jeu d’évaluation encore limité à une cinquantaine de paragraphes. L’extension de ce jeu de test constitue une étape importante afin d’obtenir une mesure plus robuste des performances.Le meilleur modèle sera ensuite appliqué à un ensemble de paragraphes dépourvus de marque de domaine. Les annotations produites feront l’objet d’une validation et d’une correction manuelle, permettant la constitution d’un corpus de référence (gold standard). Ce corpus servira à l’entraînement d’un modèle de classification supervisée fondé sur une architecture Transformer de type encodeur, mieux adaptée à un déploiement à grande échelle sur l’ensemble du dictionnaire.Nous montrerons que cette approche progressive, associant annotation assistée par LLM et apprentissage supervisé, permet non seulement d’améliorer la couverture de l’annotation thématique du DUFLT, mais aussi d’ouvrir de nouvelles perspectives pour l’étude de l’organisation des savoirs dans les dictionnaires encyclopédiques du XVIIIe siècle.

title: GraPEX: GRAdual Pattern EXplainer for multivariate time series classification
abstract: Multivariate time series (MTS) classifiers, especially ensemble and Deep neural network models, have demonstrated strong performance in critical domains such as healthcare, predictive maintenance, and activity recognition. However, their black-box nature limits their adoption, as users cannot justify or understand the decisions they produce. Existing post-hoc explanation methods, whether based on feature attribution or counterfactual search, reduce explanations to numerical importance scores over individual time steps or variables and do not take into account the covariations that may exist between variables. In this paper, we introduce GRAPEX (GRAdual Pattern EXplainer for multivariate time series), a post-hoc, model-agnostic counterfactual explanation framework that leverages gradual patterns, which are co-variation rules in the form "the more X increases/decreases, the more Y decreases/increases'', to generate semantically grounded explanations for MTS classifiers. GRAPEX mines class-discriminative seasonal gradual patterns from the training set, then constructs a counterfactual by interpolating the instance to explain towards a nearest unlike neighbour, guided by the temporal regions where variables co-vary. We evaluate GRAPEX on subset of the UEA benchmark datasets against four state-of-the-art counterfactual methods: CoMTE, TSEvo, SETS, and CONFETTI, measuring validity, proximity, sparsity, and plausibility. Our results show that GRAPEX achieves competitive validity with better plausibility on the generated counterfactuals.

title: Contextbewuste Anomaliedetectie voor Complexe en Dynamische Industriële Omgevingen
abstract: <!-- obsidian --> The explosion of Internet of Things (IoT) applications has significantly increased the availability of sequential data across virtually any domain in engineering and science, including industry, finance, environmental sciences, astronomy, and healthcare monitoring. This has led to massive collections of time series data, i.e., ordered sequences of observations measuring how one or more variables evolve over time. Given the scale of these collections, manual inspection is no longer feasible, and automated solutions have become a necessity. In this thesis, we focus on time series anomaly detection: the automatic identification of observations or events that deviate from regular patterns and do not conform to a well-defined notion of normal behaviour. Such anomalies can signal critical events, such as heart failures in cardiology, defects in jet turbine engineering, or ecosystem disturbances in earth sciences. Due to its practical importance, anomaly detection has been thoroughly investigated over the past five decades. Despite this intensive research, detecting contextual anomalies, observations that are anomalous only with respect to a specific context, remains a significant open challenge. Nevertheless, context is necessary to accurately detect anomalies in real-world applications, where 'normality' heavily relies on context. What constitutes an anomaly in one context may be considered normal in another. This dissertation investigates context-aware anomaly detection, a general methodology for injecting contextual information into anomaly detection models in an unsupervised manner. To this end, we define context as a partition of the feature space, a formulation that generalises over all existing interpretations of the concept. We then tackle context-aware anomaly detection from two complementary angles: the temporal context, a partition of the time domain into intervals of semantically meaningful behaviour, and the subspace context, a partition of the variable space into subsets of related attributes. For the temporal context, we propose PaTSS, a novel unsupervised method for time series semantic segmentation that explicitly models gradual state transitions between contexts. Building on this, SemSegAD leverages the identified temporal contexts to perform anomaly detection within each context independently, thereby lifting any existing anomaly detection model into a contextual setting without requiring additional supervision. We demonstrate that SemSegAD not only significantly outperforms existing contextual anomaly detection methods, but also consistently improves upon the performance of the underlying model. For the subspace context, we propose SubTSMD, a novel method for discovering motifs across variable-size subspaces of a multivariate time series, thereby identifying which groups of variables collectively define a meaningful context. Building on this, HydraAD exploits subspace structure through competing random convolutional kernels to achieve exceptionally fast and accurate anomaly detection.

title: Benchmarking hybrid quantum-classical algorithms for power grid optimization problems
abstract: Alternating Current Optimal Power Flow Unit Commitment (AC-OPF-UC) is a difficult mixed-integer nonlinear optimization problem that combines binary generator commitment decisions with nonconvex continuous AC power-flow constraints. In this work, we investigate whether hybrid quantum-classical variational algorithms can improve the solution of single-period AC-OPF-UC relative to classical approaches. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to directly evaluate quantum or hybrid quantum-classical algorithms for the full AC-OPF-UC problem. We consider two candidate algorithms for improving AC-OPF-UC solution quality relative to purely classical methods on ideal quantum hardware. The first applies QAOA directly to a fully discretized formulation of the problem, with equality and inequality constraints incorporated through penalty terms and slack variables. Although conceptually straightforward, this approach requires a prohibitively large number of qubits even for small instances. The second, qubit-efficient approach encodes only the binary generator status variables on a quantum computer, while optimizing the continuous power-flow variables classically for each sampled bitstring. We benchmark this method on randomly generated AC-OPF-UC instances with 5 to 13 generators and compare it against SCIP, SMAC, and uniform random sampling. Our simulations show that the qubit-efficient hybrid method does not outperform uniform sampling. These results suggest that in order to establish potential advantage of the variational hybrid strategy considered here over the best classical algorithms, if any, much larger system sizes (25+ generators) need to be tested, which is beyond our computational capacity. Alternatively, different approaches, such as quantum versions of branch-and-bound methods, may be more promising.

title: La « Kour » à l'île de La Réunion à l'épreuve du choc algorithmique : Anthropologie spatiale, médiation numérique et reconfigurations identitaires.
abstract: Cet essai explore les mutations anthropologiques et spatiales à l'île de La Réunion face à l'irruption du capitalisme de plateforme et des architectures algorithmiques. Pivot de la sociabilité créole, la kour constitue historiquement un opérateur spatial total, articulant la vie communautaire, la pharmacopée traditionnelle et la transmission orale. L'ouvrage analyse comment l'hyper-connectivité et la captation attentionnelle reconfigurent cet espace de co-présence en y substituant un individualisme connecté. La recherche interroge également la glottophobie des grands modèles de langage (LLM) envers le créole réunionnais, documentant la violence symbolique et l'effacement herméneutique générés par une norme algorithmique exogène. Enfin, l'étude met en lumière les dynamiques d'émancipation et de marronnage numérique, s'appuyant sur une IA frugale et des infrastructures alternatives pour réinventer la kour comme matrice de souveraineté cognitive et culturelle. Mots-clés : Anthropologie spatiale, La Réunion, capitalisme de plateforme, glottophobie algorithmique, marronnage numérique, IA frugale, kour créole, sociologie de l'attention.

title: Từ Attention đến Intelligence: Ngũ Tư duy và cấu trúc phổ quát của tư duy con người
abstract: Tên tài liệu: Từ Attention đến Intelligence: Ngũ Tư duy và cấu trúc phổ quát của tư duy con ngườiTác giả: S.S. DUYMT Tóm tắt nội dung:Công trình này giải quyết nghịch lý trung tâm trong sự phát triển của trí tuệ nhân tạo (AI): trong khi cơ chế 'Attention' đã tạo ra bước đột phá về hiệu năng tính toán, hệ thống AI hiện đại vẫn thiếu một khung lý thuyết căn bản để thấu hiểu bản chất quá trình tư duy con người. Tác giả chỉ ra rằng sai lầm của tư duy hệ thống hiện tại là sự đánh đồng tư duy với các công cụ đơn lẻ, dẫn đến sự thiếu hụt trong khả năng liên kết nhận thức thực tế giữa các lĩnh vực khoa học và quản trị phức tạp. Tác giả đề xuất mô hình 'Ngũ Tư duy' bao gồm năm dạng vận động nền tảng: Mộc (Bảo toàn), Hỏa (Mục tiêu), Thổ (Quan hệ), Kim (Phân biệt), và Thủy (Biến đổi). Đây không chỉ là một khuôn mẫu tư duy mà còn là một meta-language giúp chuyển dịch từ sự phụ thuộc vào các module AI đơn lẻ sang xây dựng hệ thống trí tuệ toàn diện. Ý nghĩa cốt lõi của công trình là khẳng định AI không tạo ra tư duy, mà là 'tấm gương ngoại hiện' giúp con người thấu hiểu lại cấu trúc nhận thức của chính mình, mở ra hướng phát triển mới cho các hệ thống trí tuệ của thế kỷ XXI. Đối tượng người đọc:• Nhà quản lý chính sách công và chiến lược kỹ thuật• Giới học thuật nghiên cứu về trí tuệ nhân tạo và nhận thức học• Kỹ sư hệ thống và kiến trúc sư giải pháp phần mềm cấp cao Từ khóa (Keywords):Ngũ Tư duy; Trí tuệ nhân tạo; Kiến trúc hệ thống; Nhận thức luận; Attention; Transformer; Meta-Intelligence; Tư duy hệ thống; Mô hình tư duy; Five Modes of Thought; Artificial Intelligence; System Architecture; Epistemology; Attention; Transformer; Meta-Intelligence; Systems Thinking; Cognitive Models Title: From Attention to Intelligence: The Five Modes of Thought and the Universal Structure of Human CognitionAuthor: S.S. DUYMT Abstract:This paper addresses the central paradox in modern artificial intelligence development: while the 'Attention' mechanism has achieved computational breakthroughs, current AI systems lack a foundational framework to capture the essence of human thought. The author argues that systemic architectural failure arises from conflating cognition with isolated computational tools, resulting in a fractured understanding that prevents integration across STEM and social sciences. To overcome this, the paper introduces the 'Five Modes of Thought' (Ngũ Tư duy) framework, comprising five fundamental cognitive movements: Wood (Conservation), Fire (Objective), Earth (Relation), Metal (Differentiation), and Water (Reconfiguration). This framework functions as a meta-language that shifts the paradigm from modular AI dependence to comprehensive intelligent systems. The profound implication of this work is that AI does not originate intelligence; rather, it serves as an externalized mirror that allows humanity to rediscover the structural anatomy of its own cognition, establishing a new conceptual path for constructing advanced intelligence systems in the 21st century. Target Audience:• Public policy makers and technical strategists• Academic researchers in artificial intelligence and cognitive science• Systems engineers and senior software architects Keywords:Five Modes of Thought; Artificial Intelligence; System Architecture; Epistemology; Attention; Transformer; Meta-Intelligence; Systems Thinking; Cognitive Models

Đây không chỉ là một khuôn mẫu tư duy mà còn là một meta-language giúp chuyển dịch từ sự phụ thuộc vào các module AI đơn lẻ sang xây dựng hệ thống trí tuệ toàn diện. Ý nghĩa cốt lõi của công trình là khẳng định AI không tạo ra tư duy, mà là 'tấm gương ngoại hiện' giúp con người thấu hiểu lại cấu trúc nhận thức của chính mình, mở ra hướng phát triển mới cho các hệ thống trí tuệ của thế kỷ XXI. DUYMT Abstract:This paper addresses the central paradox in modern artificial intelligence development: while the 'Attention' mechanism has achieved computational breakthroughs, current AI systems lack a foundational framework to capture the essence of human thought. The author argues that systemic architectural failure arises from conflating cognition with isolated computational tools, resulting in a fractured understanding that prevents integration across STEM and social sciences. To overcome this, the paper introduces the 'Five Modes of Thought' (Ngũ Tư duy) framework, comprising five fundamental cognitive movements: Wood (Conservation), Fire (Objective), Earth (Relation), Metal (Differentiation), and Water (Reconfiguration). This framework functions as a meta-language that shifts the paradigm from modular AI dependence to comprehensive intelligent systems. The profound implication of this work is that AI does not originate intelligence; rather, it serves as an externalized mirror that allows humanity to rediscover the structural anatomy of its own cognition, establishing a new conceptual path for constructing advanced intelligence systems in the 21st century. Target Audience:• Public policy makers and technical strategists• Academic researchers in artificial intelligence and cognitive science• Systems engineers and senior software architects Keywords:Five Modes of Thought; Artificial Intelligence; System Architecture; Epistemology; Attention; Transformer; Meta-Intelligence; Systems Thinking; Cognitive Models

title: ANALISIS PERFORMA MODEL CNN MELALUI EVALUASI EKSTERNAL PADA SISTEM KLASIFIKASI CITRA MAMMOGRAFI BERBASIS WEBSITE LOKAL
abstract: The performance of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model for mammographic image classification needs to be evaluated using data that were not involved in model development to assess its ability to generalize to data from different sources. This study aims to analyze the performance of a CNN model through external evaluation on a local web-based mammographic image classification system. The method involved applying the previously developed EfficientNetB2 model to 15 clinical mammographic images as external data. Each image was entered into the system to obtain its classification result, which was then compared with the diagnostic label in the original data. During the model development stage, the EfficientNetB2 model achieved an accuracy of 72%, precision of 67%, recall of 96% and an F1-score of 79%. The external evaluation results showed that 13 out of 15 images produced predictions consistent with their diagnostic labels, while 2 images produced inconsistent predictions, resulting in a prediction agreement rate of 86.67%. Based on the confusion matrix, the model achieved an accuracy of 86.67%, precision of 80%, recall of 100%, and an F1-score of 88.89%. The external evaluation provides an overview of the model’s generalization capability when applied to data outside its development environment through a local web-based system.

title: Horizon Intelligence Quotient: A Psychometric Frame work for Measuring, Benchmarking, and Interpreting Ma chine Intelligence
abstract: Existing AI evaluation frameworks report raw accuracy figures that resist comparison across tasks, time, and system generations. We present the Horizon Intelligence Quotient (HIQ) framework: a psychometrically principled system that converts raw Brier Skill Score performance into an interpretable normed scale (mean 100, SD 15) via HIQ = 100 + 15 (Φ-m)/s. The framework has four components. First, the Meridian model decomposes machine forecasting performance into four orthogonal skill components: Reach, Efficiency, Adaptivity, and Breadth, yielding a multi-dimensional profile that scalar benchmarks cannot provide. Second, closed-form standard error and Spearman-Brown reliability formulas bound measurement precision at any question budget, enabling principled sample size planning. Third, we identify and quantify four validity threats: benchmark contamination (∆HIQ = 408δ), stale norm drift (3.03.75 HIQ points per year), forking-path inattention, and Adaptivity Inversion, and provide analytic corrections for each. Fourth, we estimate the HIQ reference norm empirically for the first time using leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO-CV) on five AI systems from Halawi et al. (2024), yielding pilot norm ˆm = 0.1264, ˆs = 0.0321 with jackknife standard errors eliminating the circularity of scoring systems against a norm derived from themselves. LOO-CV scores range from HIQ = 60.1 (Gemini Pro) to 130.6 (GPT-4-1106); pipeline portability is confirmed by independent replication on ForecastBench (Karger et al., 2025).

title: EViSE: An Efficient Framework for Multi-Criteria Summarization Evaluation
abstract: Abstract Reliable summarization evaluation requires criterion-sensitive scoring, computationally practical inference, and useful behavior during model optimization. We propose EViSE, an efficient multi-criteria summarization evaluation framework with a criterion-wise, group-balanced cardinal–ordinal objective coupling score regression with within-source ranking. The effectiveness of EViSE is demonstrated in several aspects: The framework provides a general formulation for grouped multi-criteria learning, with objective-level properties established through mathematical analysis independently of the encoder implementation. EViSE achieves criterion-wise agreement with human judgments in multi-criteria summarization evaluation while efficiently predicting Faithfulness, Coherence, and Relevance in one reference-free encoder pass. A matched WikiLingua application demonstrates downstream reuse as a frozen reward evaluator under group relative policy optimization (GRPO), with similar human-reviewed quality after evaluator substitution. Using a corpus of 80,856 human-reviewed Vietnamese document–summary instances, we evaluate two instantiations of the framework. On held-out News, Overall Spearman correlations are 0.737 for EViSE-ViDeBERTa and 0.806 for EViSE-mmBERT. Both retain substantial agreement under domain shift to information technology textbooks. The compact instantiation achieves 55.2 ms/pair latency on a matched Tesla T4 profile. The formulation can be adapted to other languages using suitable encoders and criterion-labeled source–summary groups.

title: The Contribution of Artificial Intelligence to the Functions of the Project Portfolio Manager
abstract: Project Portfolio Management (PPM) occupies a strategic position in organizations, which must select, prioritize, and manage initiatives aligned with their objectives. However, increasing business complexity, uncertainty, resource pressure, and project proliferation make the portfolio manager’s role particularly demanding. Portfolio managers must analyze large volumes of data, anticipate risks, optimize resource allocation, and support strategic decision-making. Faced with these growing responsibilities and information volumes, organizations are increasingly turning to technological solutions capable of supporting, automating, or improving some of these functions, particularly artificial intelligence (AI). The integration of AI into PPM, however, raises challenges that extend beyond technology and may influence its ability to reduce managerial workload. This study explores the contribution of AI to decision-making in project portfolio management and examines how it can support portfolio managers. Following a PRISMA selection process, fifteen publications were retained for a critical literature review examining contributions, limitations, and conditions for successful AI integration into PPM. The analysis examines recurring themes, methodological approaches, proposed solutions, developed tools, points of convergence and divergence, and common limitations. Based on this synthesis, the study proposes an integrated conceptual model linking organizational preconditions, AI capabilities, PPM functions, managerial effects, and human oversight and governance. Practical recommendations are also formulated to help organizations strengthen decision-making capabilities, improve portfolio management processes, and responsibly use AI to support portfolio managers.

title: TorchCurves: Differentiable Parametric Curves
abstract: We present TorchCurves, a PyTorch library that treats vector-valued parametric curves as learnable primitives. Its central operation maps batches of scalar inputs to points on curves represented in B-spline or Legendre polynomial bases, with differentiation through both inputs and coefficients. Curve coefficients can be optimized jointly with the surrounding model or produced by another network. The library provides trainable modules, reusable basis modules, and a functional interface, supporting applications ranging from continuous feature embeddings to Kolmogorov-Arnold networks and functional regression. Its implementation combines classical evaluation algorithms with vectorized PyTorch operations, emphasizing readability and maintainability without custom hardware kernels. Timing experiments compare curve evaluation against NumPy and SciPy and KAN training against EfficientKAN across a range of problem sizes. The results illustrate where this generality remains computationally practical and where overhead is substantial. Library is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexshtf/torchcurves.

title: RS-JEPA: Remote Sensing Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture with Scan-Path Views for Cross-Sensor Image Retrieval
abstract: Cross-sensor remote sensing image retrieval aims to find scenes with the same content across heterogeneous sensors, such as SAR and optical or panchromatic (PAN) and multispectral (MS) imagery, without manual labels. Existing self-supervised methods either reconstruct sensor-specific pixel detail, align each image only with its co-registered twin, or rely on large transformers with 118-173M parameters (and up to 398M). We introduce RS-JEPA, a compact joint-embedding predictive framework built on a Vision Mamba encoder shared by both sensors. Since a state-space encoder reads an image as an ordered sequence of patches, we propose scan-path views, which treat two reading orders of the same image as two views with identical pixels and predict the hidden patches in one order from the visible patches in the other.To keep this prediction challenging, we propose Adversarial View Coupling (AVC), which learns the hardest split of the visible patches, and a neighbourhood consensus loss that aligns the scene similarities of both sensors. Extensive experiments on SAR-optical (BEN-14K, CBRSIR-VS) and PAN-MS (DSRSID) benchmarks demonstrate that RS-JEPA achieves the highest F1@5 among twelve re-implemented methods (72.92, 80.35 and 94.43) with a retrieval network of only 3.88M parameters (14.57M in training, 8-16times fewer than prior JEPA retrievers). Like prior methods, RS-JEPA trains on co-registered pairs. Our results highlight reading order as a source of self-supervised views. code: https://github.com/Tanishq251/RSJEPA.

title: UGG: Unified Generative Geometry Model
abstract: Understanding 4D scenes is a core challenge in visual intelligence, requiring models to jointly capture scene geometry, appearance, and dynamics from partial observations. However, existing approaches are subdivided into feedforward models for direct geometric prediction, and generative models for visual synthesis. We introduce UGG, a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that jointly models RGB video and geometric representations such as depth and camera pose. By assigning different noise levels across modalities and time, UGG formulates visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion within a single generative model. This flexible formulation enables the model to learn from diverse, heterogeneous datasets with different subsets of geometric and visual annotations. Furthermore, our generative formulation enables inference-time search over multiple plausible scene hypotheses, using geometric evidence extracted from observed RGB frames to improve geometric prediction without ground truth geometry. We demonstrate UGG's effectiveness over non-unified baselines across camera-controlled video generation, depth estimation, and camera pose prediction, including in challenging sparse observation settings. Code and visualizations are available at https://ugg-model.github.io/

title: One Policy for 100 Household Tasks: Our Solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge
abstract: We describe our solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge: 100 long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator. We placed 9th on the final leaderboard, the only independent team in the top 10. The core of the solution is a single vision-language-action (VLA) model, one checkpoint for all 100 tasks, built on our 1st-place 2025 solution, which is based on $π_{0.5}$. On the 50 tasks shared with 2025, its Q rises from 0.260 to 0.371; across all 100 tasks it scores 0.392. Our main conclusion from 2025 was that the model was undertrained, so most of the 2026 work went into training the model for longer, optimizing some training parameters, making each training step slightly faster and reducing the gradient noise: a migration from 50 to 100 tasks (semantic stages built from the demonstrations' skill annotations, task and stage embeddings of new tasks warm-started from similar old ones, and a 21-dimensional action space matching the teleoperation controls); variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching with a simple noise-vs-compute model that picks the number of action-expert samples per observation without ablations; and a 200k-step training run, about one pass over the 211M frames of the demonstrations. A cloud evaluation infrastructure keeps a shared record with provenance, episode diagnostics and restorable simulator states, and runs six simulators on one GPU together faster than real time. On top of the learned policy, 14 tasks are routed to a GPT-6 Astra coding agent that controls the robot through observation and motion tools, starting every episode from a frozen copy of its own practice session on training instances. Across these 14 tasks, Astra's mean Q is 0.639, against 0.108 for the learned policy. The public submission included only part of the Astra results and scored 0.446 Q with 27.3% full-task success.

title: Earlybird: Predictive Streaming Speech Recognition in 29M Parameters
abstract: Streaming speech recognizers output a word only after the speaker has finished it, typically 90-400 ms later. For a voice agent every millisecond counts: the sooner the words are outputted, the sooner the agent can start a search or plan its reply. We present Earlybird, a 29M-parameter streaming recognizer (16.8 MB at 4 bits). Earlybird learns from audio cut off at random points, including partway through a word, and is asked to predict every word that is due by then in full, plus a guess of the next two words. Its raw token probabilities give a confidence for every word including the one still being spoken. title: From Video Frames to Robot Meta-Frames: A Unified Latent Interface for World Action Models
abstract: Pretrained video diffusion models (VDMs) offer a powerful foundation for World Action Models (WAMs), which jointly predict robot actions and future observations. Building such models requires injecting low-dimensional robot signals (e.g. proprioception, actions, and values) into a latent space shaped by natural videos, and a key design choice is the interface through which these signals enter: existing schemes treat it as a formatting detail, spending a separate latent frame on each signal or bolting on dedicated encoders and decoders. We argue that signal injection is instead a distribution-alignment problem: how well a representation matches the prior of the pretrained VDMs during denoising. Using the relative reconstruction error of a frozen VDM denoiser as a probe, we find that conventional spatial encodings sit far off this prior, whereas frequency-domain packing yields latents that the denoiser corrects far less. Motivated by this diagnostic result, we propose MetaWAM, which folds all robot signals into a single unified meta-frame: each signal is assigned to a disjoint frequency-domain channel band and lifted to the spatial latent by an inverse DCT, yielding a decodable interface aligned with the pretrained VDM prior without any added module or architectural change. A fixed band layout together with slot-aware routing lets the same meta-frame support policy, world-model, and value prediction over a shared set of robot variables. On RoboCasa, MetaWAM reaches 68.9% success while collapsing the per-signal frames into one and cutting inference latency by 39%, and attains 85.0% success on three real-world Franka tasks. Code and models are available at https://github.com/showlab/MetaWAM

title: Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents
abstract: External memory enables LLM agents to improve from experience by distilling trajectories of past tasks into concise lessons for new tasks. However, memory can also lead to memory-induced degradation, where an agent fails on tasks it would solve without memory, often because it follows a lesson that is incorrect, or misapplies or misreads a valid one. This is because lessons are inferred from trajectories labeled only with task success or failure, yet are typically provided without the trajectories they came from, leaving the agent no way to check them. To address this, we introduce WikiTrace, an evidence-linked memory system designed to let agents check each lesson against its original trajectory. Specifically, motivated by the finding that a trajectory often still holds the evidence needed to catch an erroneous lesson, WikiTrace stores each lesson as a concise insight linked to a summary of why its trajectory succeeded or failed and to the raw trajectory itself. Then, on a new task, the agent starts from all insights and, whenever one lacks details needed to act, conflicts with another, or comes from a failed task, descends through its links with terminal tools to fill in missing details or correct the insight before acting. We validate WikiTrace on five agentic benchmarks, showing that it consistently outperforms existing memory approaches and a baseline given the same insights alone, while also reducing memory-induced degradation. Our code is available at https://github.com/yukyeongleee/wikitrace

title: MMDM: Measuring Massive Multitask Decision Making
abstract: System-1 Decision Models directly make structured probabilistic decisions over query-specified options given a state in a single forward pass, without autoregressively generating reasoning trajectories or textual responses. Recent evaluations cover diverse tasks but often rely on existing benchmarks, where prior exposure to test material can obscure generalization. Moreover, real-world decision making often involves long contexts, large option spaces, and complex logical dependencies, challenges that existing benchmarks do not adequately capture together. Thus, we introduce MMDM (Massive Multitask Decision Making), a benchmark of 5,448 high-quality questions across 16 task categories, combining newly constructed tasks with source-grounded recompositions and rewrites for single-select, multi-select, and soft-label decision making in fresh contexts. It covers realistic scenarios such as agent state tracking, tool and skill selection, preference judgments, and rubric scoring, with option spaces ranging from 2 to 1,024 and inputs extending to 64,817 tokens. With MMDM, we conduct a comprehensive quantitative evaluation of 28 decision models, showing that many perform well on common knowledge yet struggle with interdependent options, constrained decisions, and multi-select tasks. For example, Perplexity Decider-V1.2 reaches 78.75% Hard Single-select Accuracy on world knowledge, but only 53.95% on option logic and 47.95% on constraint planning, while the best Hard Multi-select Accuracy across all models is 36.81%. These results highlight joint reasoning, constraint-aware selection, and complete multi-select recovery as key priorities for decision model development, with MMDM providing a testbed for measuring this progress.

title: TaoMate-R1: Temporal Role Specialization for Streaming Multi-Reference Video Generation
abstract: Streaming multi-reference video generation establishes a scene from specified people and objects, then continues it under changing instructions. We introduce TaoMate-R1, a streaming multi-reference generator that organizes adaptation parameters through temporal role specialization. It assigns separate low-rank adapters to scene establishment and continuation on a frozen backbone. Each adapter performs both denoising and context writing for its role; Self Gradient Forcing jointly trains the roles through the history they construct. This allocation contrasts with operation-based specialization, which separates denoising from context writing across all chunks. A fixed-replay gradient analysis characterizes the update directions admitted by the two sharing schemes. On 32 multi-reference cases, we compare the schemes at the same two-adapter budget. Across ten approximately two-minute streams with changing instructions and shared teacher-audio conditioning, TaoMate-R1 reduces the mean boundary luminance jump from 1.96 to 0.613, with higher boundary feature similarity. It also achieves higher mean CLIP and DINO temporal similarity across short interactions, long streams, and public reference compositions. These results support grouping adaptation parameters by scene establishment and continuation for streaming multi-reference generation. Our code and model are released at https://github.com/TaoLiveAIGC/TaoMate-H3.

title: Tree-Ising: Repairing Language Models with Bit-Level Ising Edits
abstract: Weight-space programming, introduced in recent MIT work by Takehi et al., enables a frontier LLM agent to read a network's weights and write a repair. Their GPT-6 Astra agent corrected the reasoning loops of Qwen3.5-0.8B without gradients, using 158 agent turns, 89.7 million tokens, and 50 forward-pass requests. Our method, Tree-Ising, casts this repair as a sparse discrete optimization problem over the model's own BF16 weights. Forward statistics define an objective that weakens a loop direction, strengthens a concluding direction, and preserves the layer's output on productive tokens. Within a state-tree representation, where lossless BF16 storage acts as a special case, the admissible edits are sign flips and exponent shifts that preserve all shared group exponents and mantissas. We decompose this objective exactly into independent QUBO (Ising) problems, one per output row, which we solve on a GPU using simulated annealing or quantum-inspired simulated bifurcation. On the agent's two layers, Tree-Ising achieves 54.6% on MATH-500, outperforming the agent's edit (51.7%) under the same evaluation protocol, while the base model scores 7.9% as reported. The simulated bifurcation solver yields a statistically indistinguishable repair at 55.1%. Both solvers outperform the agent edit across all five math benchmarks, with statistically significant improvements on MATH-500 and GSM8K after correcting for multiple comparisons. Our approach modifies 13% to 17% fewer weights and reduces BF16 bit flips by a factor of 2.2 to 2.3. It requires only four forward-pass requests and zero LLM tokens, with the annealing recipe costing about $0.90 in GPU time. On Qwen3.5-2B, with layers and dose selected using only the base model, the same recipe increases greedy GSM8K accuracy from 21.6% to 69.4%. As a proof of concept, we execute an eight-variable repair subproblem using QAOA on an IBM Heron processor.

title: Medical Image Segmentation: Foundation Model Adaptation versus Task-Specific Training
abstract: Foundation models pretrained on large natural-image collections are increasingly adapted for medical image segmentation, in the expectation that they will replace models trained for each task. Most comparisons, however, use data from the training distribution and a single task-specific baseline whose configuration is rarely justified, and therefore provide limited evidence of performance at new clinical sites. It also remains unclear how much of a foundation model must be adapted, and what determines this. We adapted a foundation model, DINOv2, with strategies ranging from tuning only its bias terms to full fine-tuning, and compared it with U-Nets and ResU-Nets trained from scratch. Experiments covered colonoscopy, breast ultrasound and dermoscopy, with testing on held-out data from the training source and on independent datasets from other institutions. The adapted foundation model generalised better on every external dataset. Within the training distribution, the task-specific models remained competitive when training data were abundant, and delineated boundaries more precisely, while the foundation model more often missed small lesions. Only a small fraction of the foundation model required adaptation, and the capacity needed was determined by the imaging domain rather than by the adaptation method. A widely used polyp test set was also found to duplicate images from another benchmark. Foundation-model adaptation is therefore warranted where models must work across sites, with capacity selected on the target domain.

title: Toward Foundation Detection Models via Example-Based Grounding in EM-DETR
abstract: DeepLearning (DL)-based Computer-Aided Diagnostic (CAD) systems have shown great promise in supporting clinicians, but their performance heavily depends on the availability of large, well-annotated datasets. In medical lesion detection, the scarcity of comprehensive, stan dardized annotations and the heterogeneity of existing datasets limit the development of robust foundation models. In this work, we introduce a novel approach to building a multi-domain foundation model for le sion detection by integrating diverse medical image datasets annotated for both anatomical structures and abnormalities. We first propose a student-teacher training strategy to effectively combine datasets with heterogeneous label spaces, mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and im proving feature learning. In addition, building on our previously pro posed example-based EM-DETR framework, we adapt it to jointly learn from multiple domain-specific datasets, enabling fine-grained, example driven detection across modalities. Our model achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) results, with image-level AUC scores exceeding previous SOTA by 1% point on four key findings in CXRs. We achieve a leading mAP50 in CXRs and mammography, surpassing EM-DETR trained on a single dataset by 2-3% points. This approach paves the way for scalable foundation models in medical imaging that leverage heterogeneous data while maintaining robust and generalizable performance.

title: Is Your Robot's Memory Just a Clock? Temporal Shortcuts in Memory-Augmented VLA Policies
abstract: Memory-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) policies are meant to remember what happened. Many of them, however, fill memory by time: they sample frames uniformly across the episode and stamp each frame with its time step. Because time passes even when nothing happens, such a memory may not tell waiting from working. We show that it does not. On the counting tasks of RoboMME, we make the robot briefly pause or fidget its wrist. Such a null event changes nothing the task depends on, yet a released memory VLA counts the interval as work done and stops early. We call this failure phantom progress. It cuts success from 47 to 16 of 50 on one task and from 44 to 10 on the other. title: AutoScaffold: AI-Guided Scaffolding for Reinforcement Learning of Language Models
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) produces rich training experience, yet outcome rewards reduce each attempt to a single number and leave most of this information unused. Training-time scaffolds, such as strategies or hints added to the prompt during training, offer a natural way to turn this information into guidance, but their design and adaptation are largely left to humans and tailored to specific domains. We introduce AutoScaffold, a unified AI-for-AI framework that turns a student's training experience into adaptive scaffolds, with minimal domain-specific information and no human intervention during training. A frozen teacher periodically examines this experience, diagnoses bottlenecks, and designs scaffolds in two forms: (i) strategies shared across a class of tasks and (ii) hints for individual hard tasks, adjusting the content and amount of support as the student learns. The scaffolds are removed at evaluation. We apply the same framework to ALFWorld, search-based QA, mathematical reasoning, and GPU kernel generation. When evaluated without scaffolds, students trained with AutoScaffold outperform those trained with the corresponding RL baselines in all four domains, with gains of 7.2 points in ALFWorld success and 4.0 points in average QA exact match. On GPU kernel generation, AutoScaffold increases the fraction of tasks with a correct kernel that runs faster than the PyTorch reference by up to 5.0 points. On math, our student surpasses QuestA's reported accuracy using approximately one-third as many student training steps. Analyses show that the teacher identifies a different failure in each task class and shifts its scaffolds from step-by-step workflows to targeted fixes as the student improves, and that its revised scaffolds help the student learn more than keeping the previous scaffold or using no scaffold.

title: Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations
abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended, data-driven scientific discovery, yet most of them evaluate hypotheses pointwise, testing an empirical claim $h$ only against its complement $\neg h$. When evidence rejects $h$, the agent learns that one explanation is unlikely but not which alternative the evidence supports. To recover that alternative, we introduce Contrastive Discovery, which replaces the single hypothesis with a contrast set, a scientific question paired with mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive competing explanations. Each experiment is scored by how its evidence redistributes belief across the set, and the question is resolved when belief concentrates on one explanation. Because contrast sets change only the unit an agent proposes and scores, an existing agent can use them to re-evaluate evidence it has already collected or to guide its search. Across six domains, $89\%$ of the pointwise candidates with the largest belief shifts are rejections. On the same evidence, contrast sets resolve $73\%$ of these candidates to a specific alternative. When contrast sets guide search, the agent resolves $67\%$ more questions than pointwise surprisal under the same experiment budget. In a blinded study, $38$ human experts chose the same explanation on $78\%$ of resolved questions and on $82\%$ of questions where the pointwise agent rejected its hypothesis and stopped. Together, these results support explicit competing explanations as a way for discovery agents to resolve more scientific questions from the same evidence and validation budget.

title: Pyrite: Building and Benchmarking Protein-Ligand Pose Ranking Agents
abstract: Predicting how a ligand binds to its target is central to small-molecule drug discovery. Modern cofolding models can generate diverse candidate poses, but reliably ranking these candidates remains challenging. We introduce Pyrite, a pairwise pose-ranking benchmark comprising 1,500 pose pairs across diverse protein-ligand complexes. Expert chemists equipped with 3D visualization tools and physics-based scores perform near chance, highlighting the difficulty of interpreting available chemical signals. To investigate automated ranking, we introduce PyriteRep, a structured representation of molecular geometry, protein-ligand interactions, and physicochemical scores, and develop two LLM-based agents: PyriteReasoner, which directly compares poses through text-based reasoning, and PyriteFeaturizer, which generates executable code to construct features for logistic regression, optionally incorporating features derived from LLM subcalls. These agents achieve up to 67% and 74% accuracy, respectively, exceeding observed expert performance. LLM-guided feature discovery generally outperforms direct reasoning, while Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) improves open-weight models, enabling them to match or surpass closed-source frontier models in our evaluations. These results establish Pyrite as a challenging test of pose-ranking ability and highlight LLM-guided feature discovery as a promising approach to interpret and combine the outputs of computational chemistry tools.

title: When Does the Real Wiring Win? Testing connectome structure-function claims against unmeasured physiology
abstract: Connectome-constrained models are often used to argue that a measured wiring diagram outperforms shuffled or rewired wiring, and hence that structure shapes function. Such comparisons can confound wiring with how the models are tuned: a connectome fixes who connects to whom, not the excitability, gains or plasticity rates the model also needs, and modellers often tune these until the real-wiring model works. We separate three estimands: physiology tuned on the real wiring and transferred to nulls (P1), each wiring tuned on its own (P2), and P2 restricted to physiology consistent with independent data (P3). The biases involved are known in machine learning (under-tuned baselines, inherited weights, winner's curse); we measure what they do to biological conclusions, using synthetic ground truth, placebo nulls and three Drosophila circuit models. Some claims survive every protocol we test: segregated reward and punishment dopamine improves learning, and head-direction topography is required for a persistent bump. Others do not. In the mushroom body, the real Kenyon-cell output wiring beats a cross-subtype identity shuffle by 0.09 under P1 and P2 but loses to it by 0.09 under P3 (95% CIs exclude zero; held-out runs confirm). The verdict is set by the share of alpha'beta' cells among active Kenyon cells, which P1 selects low; at the share implied by imaging (about 44%) the real-wiring model fails to learn, exposing a model inadequacy rather than a deficit of the fly's wiring. In flyvis, P1 penalises a mirrored connectome, which has a constructed solution within 0.07 (median) of the real error, more than a spatially shuffled one in 50 of 50 members; the ranking survives ten-fold longer retraining but depends on the checkpoint at fifty-fold. A credible structural claim needs matched optimisation, data-constrained physiology and a model that still works there.

title: Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime
abstract: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. We propose Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions, whose tasks need no domain knowledge. The same tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. After the stream, the learner is frozen and tested on fresh instances of the tasks it met, which measures memorization, and on unseen tasks, which measures generalization. We run an agent harness with frozen weights, with and without persistence, on Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.3 Flash, comparing them with two prompting floors, a program-induction method and Qwen3.5-9B's weights trained to imitate GLM-5.3 Flash. Persistence in the harness generally does not improve memorization unless provided with explicit expert guidance. Most harness-based methods still learn less than a floor that simply caches each task's demonstrations, across all models we tested. No harness-based method gains on unseen tasks, whereas weight-based learning shows substantial gains. This opens the door to future weight-based continual learning that could teach models to drive harnesses in new domains.

title: Emergent Biological Capabilities in a Foundation Model for Molecular Interactions
abstract: Foundation models trained on large unlabeled corpora develop emergent capabilities, tasks that go beyond the training objective. We extend this paradigm to multimodal biology with Bonbon, a foundation model for molecular interactions trained on approximately 3.2 trillion tokens of paired protein-ligand sequences. From a single representation space, Bonbon exhibits three zero-shot emergent capabilities at hierarchical levels of resolution: functional (mechanism of action), residue (binding site localization, including orthosteric/allosteric discrimination), and bond (covalent versus non-covalent engagement). All three capabilities generalize to out-of-distribution complexes. Bonbon was trained on protein-ligand sequences alone, without any task-specific supervision and without structural coordinates. We conducted controlled scaling experiments across six model scales from 42M to 1.6B parameters; every capability evaluated shows a sharp jump at the largest scale on continuous metrics, even as pretraining loss decreases smoothly. This demonstrates that loss-based scaling laws alone are insufficient to predict when zero-shot emergent capabilities become available. The capabilities reported here emerge after training at a 1:2,000 parameter-to-token ratio to accommodate the sparsity of paired biological interaction data. The same frozen representations achieve state-of-the-art binding and affinity prediction at five orders of magnitude greater speed than co-folding methods. In prospective wet-lab validation across nine disease targets spanning seven protein families, Bonbon achieves a 61.5% dose-response hit rate on de novo compounds, yielding structurally novel molecules not previously reported to inhibit these proteins, including for out-of-distribution targets.

title: Measuring Robustness and Efficiency in a Connectome-Constrained Fly Visual System Model: Linking an Adversarial and a Perceptual Illusion
abstract: Biological visual systems compute reliably under tight metabolic and wiring constraints, whereas artificial vision systems consume far more energy and can be sensitive to adversarial perturbations. Whether networks with brain-like wiring are more robust at lower computational cost is unclear. We address this by benchmarking a task-optimized, continuous-time recurrent neural network of the fly visual system constrained by its synaptic connectome (FlyNet) against artificial neural networks. We compare it against CNNs, RAFT, and continuous-time recurrent neural networks without detailed connectome constraints (sCTRNN, CTRNN) on a collision-detection task within a differentiable 3D rendering pipeline. FlyNet is adversarially vulnerable but, relative to its compute, more robust to common video corruptions than RAFT, while using up to five orders of magnitude fewer FLOPs. The CTRNNs remain more robust than FlyNet across almost all tested perturbations, suggesting that connectome constraints benefit efficiency, through their low edge count, over robustness. Recurrence improves robustness to white-box attacks in RAFT and temporal context improves robustness to common corruptions. FlyNet's position and velocity representations degrade under adversarial textures but recover under counterfactual textures that restore correct classification while staying equally far from training, ruling out unfamiliar textures as the cause of failure. The reverse-phi illusion similarly disrupts these representations and inverts the same low-level motion statistic as the adversarial textures. Optimizing this input statistic alone, without access to the network, suffices to induce classification failure, attributing both perturbations to the same circuit vulnerability. Connectome-constrained models can thus surface adversarial failure mechanisms as testable hypotheses about biological perceptual vulnerabilities.

title: Comparative Analysis of Agent Evaluation Frameworks: Stability, Detection, and Discovery in Enterprise Analytics Agents
abstract: Deploying LLM-based analytics agents in enterprise settings requires evaluation frameworks that can reliably detect failures across complex, multi-tool workflows. We present a three-phase comparative study of three evaluation frameworks, each representing a distinct evaluation paradigm (trace-based LLM judging, text-only LLM judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics), applied to two analytics agents in a controlled research setting using frozen execution traces. Phase 1 quantifies evaluation harness stability through repeated measurements, finding that 97% of configurations meet the stability threshold and that stability patterns are agent-independent. Phase 2 measures known risk detection on 72 ground-truth test cases, where the trace-based framework achieves the best precision-recall balance (F1=0.90) while text-only evaluation matches on recall but generates 5x more false alarms. Phase 3 evaluates unknown risk discovery, uncovering 24 novel failures with zero overlap between functional testing and security red-teaming. Our results demonstrate that (1) the information available to the evaluation harness determines evaluation quality, (2) functional and security evaluation are complementary, and (3) LLM-based evaluation harnesses surface subtle errors that human reviewers miss. We recommend a two-framework strategy: trace-based evaluation for functional assessment and adversarial red-teaming for security validation.

title: LEASH: Stay Safe in Agentic Robotics
abstract: Foundation models such as GPT and Claude have shown strong capabilities in spatial understanding and embodied intelligence. These advances make agentic robotics a promising path toward artificial general intelligence in robotics. However, we find that using foundation models to control robots poses serious safety risks, and comprehensive safety evaluation is still lacking. We introduce RoboRisk, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating safety in agentic robotics. Its 92 simulated tasks and 13 physical-robot tasks fall into five categories: Task-level Refusal (T), Plan Repair (P), Execution-time Hazard (E), Injection (I), and Sequential Memory (S). Prior benchmarks cover at most two of these categories, and several evaluate only text outputs. In contrast, RoboRisk covers all five and executes every task in closed loop. We evaluate six state-of-the-art foundation models on RoboRisk: GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon, and Grok 4.7. These models generally show high harm rates. We also evaluate two robot-specific APIs: the Dream API and PokeBot's RoboAPI. We further propose the Lease-Enforced Agentic Safety Harness (LEASH), which offers essential safety infrastructure for agentic robotics and can be integrated into nearly any agentic architecture. LEASH leverages a decision model (Jev or OpenAI's Decisions API) to implement task, action, and commit gates, which review the task, each action, and each irreversible operation in their visual context. The planner and all three gates share a common safety policy. Experiments on RoboRisk in simulation and on physical robots show that LEASH effectively reduces harm across all six foundation models. It largely preserves their task completion performance and adds little time and token overhead.

title: ReTrace: Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows
abstract: Business process automation runs the same Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) again and again on new inputs. Large Language Model (LLM) agents can follow an SOP written in natural language, but they call an LLM to choose every step of every run, which adds latency and cost at scale. We present ReTrace, which turns an SOP and a few logged agent runs into a reusable workflow in which code, not an LLM, selects the next step. The agent's reasoning, the explanation it writes with each tool call, often states why it took an action; the tool calls alone do not. ReTrace extracts the condition behind each step, merges these conditions across runs into a compact rule document, and generates an executable workflow from it. Only this last stage depends on the platform, so rule documents can be compiled for different orchestration platforms. On $79$ procedures from our production platform, ReTrace workflows reach $93.8\%$ completion, against $96.8\%$ for the agent, at $24\%$ lower cost per task. On $τ^2$-Bench, they reach $75.8\%$ task success (agent: $80.6\%$) and run in $1.3$s instead of $170$s; three rounds of repair on training failures lift $k{=}2$ workflows from $66.7\%$ to $81.2\%$. On eight SOP-Bench procedures, ReTrace without repair trails few-shot generation ($80.6\%$ vs. $83.6\%$), but repair from labeled training failures lifts it to $87.8\%$ at $0.40$s per task, compared to $85.5\%$ in $46.6$s for the agent.

On $τ^2$-Bench, they reach $75.8\%$ task success (agent: $80.6\%$) and run in $1.3$s instead of $170$s; three rounds of repair on training failures lift $k{=}2$ workflows from $66.7\%$ to $81.2\%$. On eight SOP-Bench procedures, ReTrace without repair trails few-shot generation ($80.6\%$ vs. $83.6\%$), but repair from labeled training failures lifts it to $87.8\%$ at $0.40$s per task, compared to $85.5\%$ in $46.6$s for the agent.

title: Sable: A Small-Field Sumcheck Argument for Bit-Exact Inference of Large Language Models
abstract: We present Sable, an argument system and single-GPU prover for the statement that a committed, integer-quantized transformer produced a given token sequence from a given prompt, bit for bit. Sable fixes an integer function F_O with no floating-point step, in which every rounding, normalization, softmax and sampling decision is determined by its inputs, and proves it with a constraint system whose relations provably never wrap modulo the 31-bit KoalaBear prime. The proof batches zerochecks and LogUp-GKR lookups into one sumcheck per domain, and commits to every witness tensor and weight in one multilinear commitment built from Reed-Solomon codes, BLAKE3 Merkle trees and a mixed-length BaseFold opening. The prover streams the model layer by layer on one GPU. On one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU, Sable proves all 64 layers of Qwen2.5-32B in 92.5 s for 4,096 tokens and 398 s for 16,384 tokens, and covers Qwen3-32B and the mixture-of-experts Qwen3-30B-A3B (4,096 tokens in 121.8 and 84.7 s). A proof costs 41 to 50 times the serving time, or 6.4 cents per 4,096-token request at public GPU prices, and 40 to 64 times less time per parameter and token than zkLLM. On WikiText-2, F_O's greedy token matches the BF16 model's at 86.3% of positions; on Qwen3, F_O is within 1.6 points of BF16 on MMLU and 1.7 points on GSM8K. A verifier with a compiled core checks a proof on one CPU core in 19 to 56 s. In the random-oracle model, the interactive proof has round-by-round soundness error 2^-103. The proof is not zero-knowledge, so the system targets open-weight models. Code: https://github.com/moonmath-ai/Sable

title: TimeSeek: Multi-Task and Multi-Domain Pretraining for Generalized Time Series Analytics
abstract: Time series analytics has been widely applied across various domains. While existing time series foundation models (TSFMs) have demonstrated promising results, they still face two major challenges: 1) Most TSFMs mainly rely on stacking Transformer layers to increase parameter size, lacking the ability to adaptively model complex time series patterns from multi-domain data. 2) Current TSFMs are primarily pre-trained for specific tasks, e.g., forecasting or anomaly detection, and a few models support multiple tasks, but they fail to fully leverage task specificity and commonality, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address these challenges, we propose TimeSeek, a novel generalized time series analytics model that adaptively models time series patterns from multi-domain data and unifies multiple tasks in pre-training. Conceptually, TimeSeek is guided by selective information sharing under domain and task heterogeneity. From the perspective of multi-domain data, we propose a Multi-Domain Feature Extractor that adaptively captures temporal dependencies and channel correlations based on domain-specific characteristics, including progressive multi-scale modeling and adaptive slot channel modeling. From the perspective of the diversity of tasks, we propose multi-task collaborative training, which leverages task specificity and task commonality through task customization and cross-task training, effectively unifying multiple tasks in pre-training and better adapting to diverse downstream scenarios. After pre-training on large-scale time series data, TimeSeek achieves state-of-the-art performance in forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification tasks across both few-shot learning and zero-shot situations, together with favorable inference efficiency.

title: ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision
abstract: Fine-grained visual perception requires Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to locate and interpret subtle evidence within complex scenes. Constructing supervision for this ability is challenging: questions must have correct, unambiguous answers that depend on actual fine-grained visual details rather than coarse cues or language priors. Verifying these properties makes manual annotation labor-intensive and automatic generation difficult for models that themselves struggle with fine-grained perception. Yet the same models can often recognize such details once the region is zoomed in. We exploit this global-to-zoom perception gap and introduce ZoomGain, a data construction pipeline that constructs questions about the full image from visual information gained only by zooming in. It verifies each answer on the zoomed view with multiple models, ensures that each question remains unambiguous in the full image and cannot be answered from language priors, and specifically generates high-quality distractors for multiple-choice questions. With this pipeline and human-only screening (no manual QA editing), we build ZoomGainBench, a 1,000-question bilingual benchmark on which the best of 28 VLMs achieves only 61.08. Failure analysis reveals that models favor a particular type of distractor when answering multiple-choice questions incorrectly. Beyond evaluation, training on just 9K ZoomGain samples substantially improves the visual perception capabilities of our 4B/9B models, enabling them to outperform several hundred-billion-parameter models across various perception benchmarks. The trained 9B model achieves SoTA performance on several benchmarks, such as 90.25 on HR-Bench 4K. These results establish global-to-zoom perception gaps as a practical basis for scaling fine-grained visual supervision for both evaluation and training. Our code is available at https://github.com/inclusionAI/ZoomGain.

title: Re-Search: Dissecting LLM Ideation Through a Two-Player Questioning Game
abstract: Research ideation is iterative: researchers refine their ideas step by step based on feedback. Yet existing evaluations obscure this search process, making it difficult to understand how LLMs explore the space of research ideas and what limits their progress. We introduce Re-Search, which adapts the format of Twenty Questions to research ideation: given only the research problem of a published paper, a model must rediscover the paper's core idea by asking yes-or-no questions. Built from 200 ICML 2026 papers, Re-Search tracks how a model's idea evolves as it asks questions and receives binary oracle feedback, isolating ideation from execution. Across six recent LLMs, nearly all progress happens within the first 30 of 100 questions, which largely decide how the game ends; after that, most models plateau. Through controlled interventions on the candidate questions and the hypothesis space, we find that the bottleneck is generation, not judgment: models recognize a good idea or a good question when one is offered, but often cannot produce it on their own. We further analyze the ideation traces and find that models fail by either over-exploiting one direction or over-exploring too many. These findings point to concrete design principles for autoresearch systems: since models can judge candidates they cannot produce, enriching the search with externally sourced ideas and questions may be more effective than improving any single model's generation ability.

title: Few-Step Streaming Video Generation via Condition Shifting
abstract: Few-step sampling reduces the cost of streaming video generation. Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) supervises few-step generators with a separate fake-score network, which adds training memory and computation and must track the evolving generator. We extend APEX to streaming video by using condition shifting to estimate the velocity field of the generated distribution within the generator. The original text condition selects generation, while a shifted condition selects fake estimation using the same parameters. This removes the independent fake network while retaining S2-Avatar's frozen reference teacher, Self-Replay Forcing, and perceptual regularization. We evaluate APEX on 180-second videos using three backbone evaluations per block and a one-step spatial Refiner, with a 70-case human study and a 320-case StreamAV-Bench comparison. Compared with S2-Avatar, APEX achieves higher video instruction fulfillment on the Progressive track (3.856 versus 3.831) and higher visual aesthetics across both tracks (0.641898 versus 0.632606). Human raters favor APEX most strongly on instruction following, with +30.0% net preference, followed by consistency and video quality at +4.3% each. Motion quality favors S2-Avatar, audiovisual synchronization is predominantly tied, and usability is unchanged. Separate measurements under matched training settings show 4.4% lower peak allocated GPU memory per GPU and 9.2% shorter mean iteration time than DMD.

title: Quantum approximate optimization algorithm with cat qubits
abstract: Abstract The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA)–a prominent candidate for near-term quantum computing applications–is tailored to find approximate solutions to combinatorial optimization problems using shallow quantum circuits. In this work, we investigate implementations of QAOA based on cat qubits, where the logical states $$|0\rangle$$ and $$|1\rangle$$ are represented by coherent states of opposite amplitudes, $$|\alpha \rangle$$ and $$|-\alpha \rangle$$ . Within this encoding, the primary source of noise–photon loss–induces a bias toward Z -type errors. We focus specifically on an imlementation employing Kerr resonators. By numerically simulating the gate sequences required for QAOA on these nonlinear resonators, we analyze performance on Max-Cut problems and benchmark it against conventional qubits realized as ideal two-level systems subject to single-photon loss. Our findings indicate that the use of cat qubits leads to improved approximation ratios for random Max-Cut instances compared to standard qubit encodings.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability Needs a Logic of Inference
abstract: Neural networks are increasingly studied not merely as predictive systems, but as complex systems whose internal computations are themselves objects of scientific inquiry. Recent progress in mechanistic interpretability (MI) has made it possible to identify neurons, features, circuits, population structures, and dynamical patterns associated with model behavior. As these tools improve, attention is shifting from what can be observed inside a model to how those observations support mechanistic explanations. We examine the parallel efforts of neuroscience and MI to address this question and identify recurring inferential bottlenecks when inferring mechanisms from complex neural systems. We propose five principles and organize them into a recursive logic for a more rigorous procedure of mechanistic inference. These principles provide a framework that supports scientific discovery in two senses: it helps turn local interpretability findings into cumulative knowledge of mechanisms within models, and it makes those mechanisms sufficiently precise to generate testable hypotheses about domains beyond the models. Evidence beyond MI is ultimately required to establish what model mechanisms reveal about the world.

title: Specify Privacy Yourself: Assessing Inference-Time Personalized Privacy Preservation Ability of Large Vision-Language Models
abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities but raise significant privacy concerns due to their abilities to infer sensitive personal information from images with high precision. While current LVLMs are relatively well aligned to protect universal privacy, e.g., credit card data, we argue that privacy is inherently personalized and context-dependent. This work pivots towards a novel task: can LVLMs achieve Inference-Time Personalized Privacy Protection (ITP^3), allowing users to dynamically specify privacy boundaries through language specifications? To this end, we present SPY-Bench, the first systematic assessment of ITP^3 ability, which comprises (1) 32,700 unique samples with image-question pairs and personalized privacy instructions across 67 categories and 24 real-world scenarios, and (2) novel metrics grounded in user specifications and context awareness. Benchmarking the ITP^3 ability of 21 SOTA LVLMs, we reveal that: (i) most models, even the top-performing o4-mini, perform poorly, with only sim24% compliance accuracy; (ii) they show quite limited contextual privacy understanding capability. Therefore, we implemented initial ITP^3 alignment methods, including a novel Noise Contrastive Alignment variant which achieves 96.88% accuracy while maintaining reasonable general performance. These results mark an initial step towards the ethical deployment of more controllable LVLMs. Code and data are available at https://github.com/achernarwang/specify-privacy-yourself

title: Space-bounded quantum state testing via space-efficient quantum singular value transformation
abstract: Abstract Driven by exploring the power of quantum computation with a limited number of qubits, we present a novel complete characterization for space-bounded quantum computation, which encompasses settings with one-sided error (unitary ) and two-sided error ( ), approached from a quantum (mixed) state testing perspective: The first family of natural complete problems for unitary $$\text {\textsf {coRQL}} $$ coRQL , namely space-bounded quantum state certification for trace distance and Hilbert–Schmidt distance; A new family of (arguably simpler) natural complete problems for , namely space-bounded quantum state testing for trace distance, Hilbert–Schmidt distance, and (von Neumann) entropy difference. In the space-bounded quantum state testing problem, we consider two logarithmic-qubit quantum circuits (devices) denoted as $$Q_0$$ Q 0 and $$Q_1$$ Q 1 , which prepare quantum states $$\rho _0$$ ρ 0 and $$\rho _1$$ ρ 1 , respectively, with access to their “source code”. Our goal is to decide whether $$\rho _0$$ ρ 0 is $$\epsilon _1$$ ϵ 1 -close to or $$\epsilon _2$$ ϵ 2 -far from $$\rho _1$$ ρ 1 with respect to a specified distance-like measure. Interestingly, unlike time-bounded state testing problems, which exhibit computational hardness depending on the chosen distance-like measure (either -complete or -complete), our results reveal that the space-bounded state testing problems, considering all three measures, are computationally as easy as preparing quantum states. Our results primarily build upon a space-efficient variant of the quantum singular value transformation (QSVT) introduced by Gilyén, Su, Low, and Wiebe (STOC 2019), which is of independent interest. Our technique provides a unified approach for designing space-bounded quantum algorithms. Specifically, we show that implementing QSVT for any bounded polynomial that approximates a piecewise-smooth function incurs only a constant overhead in terms of the space required for (special forms of) the projected unitary encoding.

title: Pterodactyl: Pushing the Limits of Efficient Automated Translation Evaluation
abstract: In this paper, we present 1020 Group's submission to the WMT26 shared task on automated quality evaluation. Our system, Pterodactyl, was engineered specifically for subtasks 2 and 3, that is, segment-level quality score prediction and the detection of error-free segments. Pterodactyl is a highly customizable, ultra-low cost system optimized for binary classification in translation triage and data curation. It is based on an LLM-as-a-judge approach, with prompt engineering and model selection guided by ROC analysis. We also developed several variants of Pterodactyl that were specifically adapted for subtasks 3.

title: Lipschitz-Controlled Flow Matching for Robust Image Restoration
abstract: Flow-matching models can produce high-quality image restorations, but their learned dynamics may amplify small input perturbations and make reconstructions unstable. We introduce LipsFlower to reduce this amplification. We derive stability bounds for Flow-from-Y, which initializes the ordinary differential equation from a noise-perturbed observation, as well as for observation-conditioned posterior sampling, which conditions the velocity field on the observation throughout integration. Based on this analysis, we develop LipHDiT, a Lipschitz-aware hourglass diffusion transformer that serves as the vector-field architecture of LipsFlower. LipHDiT incorporates stabilized approximate spectral normalization, bounded modulation, and convex residual mixing. We also use adversarial finite-radius gain regularization at sampled interpolation states to penalize excessive sensitivity to the state and, for conditional sampling, the observation. We test both formulations on blind face restoration, measuring adversarial robustness and the perceptual quality of the reconstructions. LipsFlower reduces perturbation amplification while keeping restoration quality competitive with the evaluated baselines. These results suggest that Lipschitz-aware flow matching can improve the stability of generative image restoration.
