title: Compositional random forest
abstract: Compositional data have been analysed in the literature from three main points of view: directly on the simplex, in log-ratio coordinates, and as directional data on the unit sphere. In this paper, we construct a random forest framework for compositional responses that accommodates all three. Random forests are ensembles of decision trees, and the split criterion determines how each tree grows. We use the log-likelihood gain as the split criterion and consider distributions defined on the different spaces in which compositions can be represented. The Dirichlet likelihood has been studied in the literature, but its covariance is fixed by its mean up to a single scalar, and its maximum likelihood estimator has no closed form. To obtain more flexible criteria, we use two well-known transformations. First, the square-root transformation maps compositions onto the unit sphere, where existing directional distributions require numerical estimation. We introduce a tangent-normal (TN) distribution, which shares its parameters with the Kent distribution, and construct a split criterion whose gain is computed from additive sufficient statistics: the shape parameters are maximised out in closed form, up to an exponentially small truncation constant, so that no parameter is estimated iteratively. Second, the log-ratio transformation maps compositions to Euclidean space, where the multivariate logistic-normal distribution has a flexible covariance and a closed-form maximum log-likelihood, also based on additive sufficient statistics. Both criteria respond to a shift of the mean, measured relative to the covariance, and to a change in the covariance itself. In simulations, the most accurate forest depended on the covariance structure of the composition. The TN forest was the most accurate in two of the three designs.

title: Federated Learning for Cross-Regional Epidemic Forecasting with Asynchronous Outbreaks
abstract: Objective: Epidemic outbreaks are often asynchronous across regions, yet collaborative forecasting is hampered by privacy laws and heterogeneous public health interventions. We developed and evaluated, as a proof of concept, a federated learning (FL) framework for cross-regional COVID-19 forecasting under asynchronous outbreaks among Guangdong, Macau, and Portugal, while maintaining data sovereignty. Methods: Using daily case data from WHO and China CDC for the three regions, whose outbreaks were asynchronous and interventions heterogeneous, we trained Long Short-Term Memory networks via FL for short-term forecasting, benchmarked against localized and centralized training using Root Mean Square Error, Mean Absolute Error, and Symmetric Mean Absolute Percentage Error. All experiments used the Flower FL framework with consistent hyperparameters across sites. Publicly available, aggregated case-count data were used so that the centralized benchmark could be computed as a reference. Results: The dataset comprised 1,233 daily observations (411 days) of new confirmed COVID-19 cases from November 24, 2021, to January 8, 2023. The earlier Omicron wave in Portugal supplied transmission dynamics that improved forecasts in the later-onset regions of Macau and Guangdong. The FL model achieved a normalized Root Mean Square Error of 0.028, an 88.3% improvement over the local model (0.240) and comparable to the centralized model, with network overhead mainly determined by model size and aggregation rounds. Conclusion: FL achieved short-term forecasting accuracy close to centralized training while maintaining data residency, with acceptable overhead. Leveraging asynchronous outbreaks across regions may offer a practical path to privacy-preserving collaborative forecasting, though prospective validation is required.

title: Secure AI Agent Infrastructure
abstract: Reproducible research prototypes addressing one question: can an autonomous agent be trusted with a security decision, and would you know if it could not? Contains an agent verification harness that scores whether each claim in an LLM's output is supported by the documents it retrieved, a per-class smart-contract vulnerability benchmark with audited negative controls, and an LLM audit agent. Results files record measured runs against SHA-256-pinned sources; metrics that the evidence does not support are withheld with a machine-readable reason rather than reported.

title: Achieving Robust Channel Estimation Neural Networks on Doppler effects by Designed Training Data
abstract: Channel estimation is crucial in wireless communication systems. Many existing works train and test their models using the same or similar channel. However, practical channels are infinitely diverse and time-variant while data-driven algorithms often degrade on new and previously unseen channels. This prohibits the practical implementation of neural networks for channel estimation, particularly in high speed scenarios characterized by rapidly channel profile changes and very high Doppler shifts. Online training can fine-tune models to adapt to new channels, but requires high computation resource and incurs significant latency for physical-layer devices. Moreover, online training cannot exhaustively cover all possible channels because there are infinitely many possible channels. Therefore, we investigate the ability of neural networks to generalize to wireless channels. This paper proposes design criteria to generate synthetic training data, which guaranty that the resulting networks perform robustly across wireless channels, especially for very high Doppler shifts and different Doppler spectra. It ensures that offline-trained neural networks require no prior information or online training to precisely estimate the new channels. To demonstrate general applicability, we use neural networks with different levels of complexity to show that the generalization achieved appears to be independent of architecture. From simulation results, neural networks achieve a certain performance across wireless channels with different unseen power delay profiles (PDP) and Doppler shifts.

title: Physics-Constrained Autoencoder for Interpretable Health Representation Learning in Turbofan Engines
abstract: Health Indices (HIs) summarize degradation from operational data and support diagnostic and prognostic tasks in Prognostics and Health Management (PHM). Their usefulness depends on capturing degradation and interpreting system condition. Autoencoders learn such representations from unlabelled monitoring data; however, when training is driven only by reconstruction, the physical meaning of latent variables remains undefined, limiting their interpretation and diagnostic value. This work proposes a physics-constrained autoencoder that embeds system knowledge as an inductive bias in the decoder architecture and as a learning bias in the loss function. The decoder contains differentiable physical equations that receive latent variables and operating conditions as inputs, structurally guiding each latent variable to represent a predefined physical quantity and enabling component-level analysis before aggregation into a system-level HI.The methodology is benchmarked on the N-CMAPSS dataset against alternative representations. Reconstruction reaches an $R^2$ of 0.9993 and an MAE of 0.0036, comparable to fully data-driven models. After operating-condition correction, the inferred physical quantities track degradation, and their aggregation produces an HI with a Spearman correlation of 0.9791 with the ground truth, an RMSE of 0.0286, and an MAE of 0.0233. The methodology is further evaluated using a single model trained across four datasets representing distinct degradation scenarios. This model preserves component-level signatures that distinguish compression-side from expansion-side degradation without diagnostic labels.Finally, the proposed framework enables degradation trends to be visualized on component maps, providing a health representation in a form familiar to engine operators and domain experts.

title: Chain of Physics: Supporting Fault Diagnosis with Engineering-Inspired Large Language Model Reasoning
abstract: Fault diagnosis in complex systems requires linking observed changes in physical quantities to the failure mechanisms that produce them. Experienced engineers perform this task by combining sensor information with knowledge of system behavior and fault propagation. Large Language Models (LLMs) can support this process, but their diagnostic reasoning depends on the availability of asset-specific engineering knowledge and on how this knowledge is represented and used during inference. This work introduces Chain of Physics (CoP), an LLM-based fault-diagnosis framework built around a Constrained Knowledge Graph (CKG) generated automatically from asset-specific reference documentation. CoP addresses failure-sensor association from textual engineering knowledge. The CKG stores diagnostic chains connecting failure modes, changes in physical quantities, and monitoring sensors. During inference, semantically similar graph paths are retrieved for each question and used as both information and in-context examples for the reasoning process. Candidate failure modes are extracted from the question and analysed independently through dedicated LLM calls, which generate plausible failure-to-observation chains. A final decision module compares these chains with the available answer choices. CoP is evaluated on the FailureSensorIQ benchmark across four industrial asset classes and three LLMs. Compared with direct prompting and conventional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), CoP improves diagnostic accuracy across all evaluated models, with gains ranging from 7.8 to 19.6 percentage points and from 11.7 to 18.2 percentage points, respectively. The results show that structured engineering knowledge can improve LLM-based diagnostic reasoning when graph retrieval is combined with in-context examples of fault propagation.

abstract: Code, log-ID manifest and derived result tables for a study measuring the false alarm rate of the PX4 autopilot's EKF innovation gates on 1,627 real quadrotor flights, and evaluating split conformal prediction as a calibrated alternative. title: Recurrent Modular Structure in Spiking Neural Network Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Biological neural circuits are both modular and recurrent, with dense communities sparsely linked to one another. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) for reinforcement learning are usually feed-forward, and it is unclear how to obtain functional modules in a recurrent SNN or what they buy. In this work, we introduce a class of spiking networks, called Community Recurrent SNNs (CoRe SNNs): recurrent networks partitioned into communities with fixed roles. A controller community receives the stimulus, each action has its own community, and latent communities carry internal state. Spiking activity is then a walk between communities, and the action is the community the walk reaches. All learning is local and three-factor, and the recurrent communities are closer to cortical microcircuits than a feed-forward actor. We compare three regimes for obtaining the communities: dynamic modularity, in which a new learning rule we introduce, Map-STDP, encourages modular structure during learning; partial modularity, in which a stochastic block model (SBM) initialization enforces it partly; and full modularity, in which sealing enforces it fully. On CartPole, across three spiking neuron models, Map-STDP improves learning over the same network without it matches full modularity (sealed communities) on two of the three models, and makes the observed spike walk more compressible. Replacing the feed-forward actor of a TD-STDP actor-critic with recurrent action communities improves on the feed-forward network on CartPole and LunarLander, and matches it on Acrobot. How strongly to enforce modularity depends on the task: full modularity helps most on Acrobot, while on LunarLander the dynamic, partial and full regimes perform alike. Overall, these recurrent modular networks can match or even improve upon feed-forward approaches, with improvements in bio-plausibility and energy efficiency.

title: Frequency-Adaptive Flow Matching for High-Fidelity Text-to-Speech Synthesis
abstract: Flow matching (FM) enables efficient acoustic modeling for text-to-speech (TTS), but fine spectral structures may remain imperfectly reconstructed. To address this issue, we propose frequency-adaptive flow matching (FAFM), which replaces the shared linear interpolation schedule with a frequency-dependent nonlinear schedule. By assigning different interpolation exponents to Mel-frequency bands, FAFM advances high-frequency components earlier along their conditional paths while preserving the endpoints of the linear baseline. The corresponding analytical target velocity modulates frequency-dependent evolution without introducing additional network modules. Evaluations across two TTS architectures and English and Chinese datasets show improvements in spectral reconstruction and several objective quality and intelligibility metrics. Results averaged over three independent training seeds, together with band-wise spectral analysis, support the effectiveness of moderate frequency modulation. Subjective listening tests show small numerical gains in perceived naturalness over standard CFM.

title: Lilo: A Multi-Agent Conversational Sandbox for Children's Digital Communication
abstract: Children's peer conflicts increasingly play out in group chats, where tone and timing are stripped away, and a hurtful message is easier to send than to say aloud. We present Lilo, a multi-agent conversational system that lets children practice such conversations, so they are better prepared when they encounter them in real digital communication. In Lilo, the child joins two AI-driven peers mid-argument, coached by a mentor character, also named Lilo, through a Stop-Think-Act traffic light. Through an exploratory study with 28 children (aged 9-11), we examine how children engage with Lilo's simulated peer conflict and the mentor's traffic-light interventions. The study included an intervention with Lilo, surveys before and after the intervention, and exit interviews. Participants reported significantly higher self-efficacy for coping with unpleasant messages after their interaction with Lilo. They felt safe experimenting, knowing nothing they wrote would be held against them.

title: An optimized multi-transformer framework with explainable AI for racism and body-shaming detection in bangla social media
abstract: Abstract Racism and body shaming are among the most damaging forms of abuse on Bangla social media, yet they are rarely treated as distinct detection targets, and existing studies seldom report controlled comparisons, statistical validation or interpretability. This paper presents an optimized multi-transformer framework that separates racism from body shaming in Bangla text already identified as abusive. A dataset of 4,989 verified instances (2,573 body shaming, 2,416 racism; 1,214 naturally collected comments and 3,775 ChatGPT-assisted sentences) was constructed. BanglaBERT, mBERT, MuRIL and XLM-RoBERTa were fine-tuned under identical conditions with Optuna search, stratified five-fold cross-validation, exact McNemar tests and SHAP with a faithfulness evaluation. BanglaBERT achieved the highest numerical performance (96.39% accuracy at baseline, 96.79 ± 0.59% under cross-validation, 96.29% after tuning), although its differences from the other models were not statistically significant and a wider search favoured XLM-RoBERTa (97.19%). Racism was recovered less reliably than body shaming, and SHAP faithfulness ran inversely to accuracy. Additional evaluations showed stable results across seeds and under leakage-aware grouped cross-validation (96.07–96.63%), but accuracy fell to 86.60% to 89.95% on naturally collected test comments and to 55.49–63.81% when models were trained on generated sentences alone, because generation changed what each class expresses, notably racism as regional stereotyping rather than colourism. On the same data, the prior study’s support vector machine reached 89.98%, while a character n-gram support vector machine matched the transformers and exceeded them when trained on collected comments (93.16%). Validation on naturally collected comments is therefore needed before deployment.

title: Elastic-WAM: Adaptive Spatiotemporal Imagination for Efficient Robot Control
abstract: World-Action Models improve robot control by predicting future visual dynamics, but iterative video denoising incurs substantial inference overhead. Recent approaches reduce this cost through partial future denoising, yet typically rely on fixed refinement budgets. Our empirical observations reveal that preferred refinement depths vary across tasks and states, while different future regions exhibit varying relevance to action generation. Motivated by these findings, we propose Elastic-WAM, which adaptively allocates world refinement computation across temporal denoising time and spatial future space. A unified spatiotemporal refinement demand field governs when to stop world refinement, how far to advance each denoising step, and which regions to refresh. We parameterize this field with a shared temporal basis and spatial amplitudes, and learn it through a three-stage action-grounded supervised procedure. At inference, the learned field guides recurrent sparse world refinement to improve task success while reducing inference overhead. Evaluations across diverse simulation benchmarks and real-world long-horizon manipulation demonstrate state-of-the-art control performance with reduced inference latency.

title: A Cross-Scenario Survey and Analysis of Self-Evolving Multimodal Agents
abstract: Recent work shows that multimodal agents increasingly self-improve without recurring human annotation. However, each self-improvement mechanism is designed and evaluated within a single scenario, leaving its preconditions unverified under cross-scenario transfer. This survey investigates the structural source of asymmetric mechanism transfer across four scenarios: multimodal reasoning, multimodal generation, GUI and Web navigation, and embodied manipulation. We first formalize the self-evolving multimodal agent by four criteria and a differentia of self-reference, and adopt the three-stage self-evolving loop of experience generation, feedback acquisition, and update consolidation as our analytical framework to position the scenarios along ceilings on rollout count and feedback fidelity. Comparing self-evolving with fixed loops within each scenario separates the limitations that the scenario imposes from those inherent in the self-evolving design. We then recast each mechanism as a trade-off that raises a scarce factor by presupposing a task-structural resource, such as output equivalence or checkable outcomes, and judge it portable, conditional, blocked, or redundant across scenarios. We attribute the asymmetry to divergent combinations of scarce factors and resources across opposite transfer directions, and identify the matched-budget measurements that could overturn these still untested verdicts.

title: Location Matters: Sparse Latent-Variance Attacks for Face Privacy against Diffusion Personalization
abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models can learn and reproduce an individual's identity from only a few reference photos, creating risks of unauthorized and misleading content generation. Proactive defenses address this risk by adding adversarial perturbations to facial images before release, thereby disrupting identity acquisition during downstream personalization. However, existing methods typically rely on dense $L_\infty$-bounded perturbations, whose accumulated distortions can become visible around facial structures. Recent methods improve protected-image quality, but often at the cost of reduced protection effectiveness. In this paper, we propose Sparse Encoder Attack on Latent Variance (SEAL), a sparse adversarial protection framework that modifies only 5% of the spatial locations in a facial image. SEAL combines a differentiable top-k masking scheme that jointly optimizes perturbation locations and values with a variance-oriented objective over the frozen VAE encoder's latent distribution to disrupt identity-consistent representations. A saliency-guided dispersion penalty further discourages perturbation concentration in perceptually salient facial regions. Experiments on CelebA-HQ and VGGFace2 show that SEAL achieves the best protected-image quality among the compared methods, exceeding 41 dB PSNR with 0.97 SSIM and at most 0.07 LPIPS, while reducing identity similarity to at most 0.15 after diffusion personalization. These results demonstrate that sparse location optimization enables strong identity protection while preserving high visual quality. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Lvxan/SEAL

title: Semantic Chains: From Reachable Facts to Justified Answers
abstract: How can the facts that justify an answer be found from a question and presented as a sequence of connected statements? This paper models a context as a graph of logical facts and takes as given which expressions represent each fact. A parent fact can express a relation among its subfacts, and a preserving edge allows the content of a subfact to be recovered within a full representation of its parent. Suppose a root fact justifies the full answer and a path of preserving edges leads from that root to a fact that designates an object shared by the question and the answer. Under the conditions of the model, a search starting from the objects in the question reaches the root and covers every fact in the selected expansion. The root then admits a text that forms a single link connecting the question to the full answer and justifying it. For chains with several links, the paper gives a complete enumeration of candidate orders within the stated class and specifies when the link texts jointly preserve the justification and support every transition.

title: Comparative evaluation of ResNet-Based AI models for breast cancer detection in digital mammography and digital breast tomosynthesis
abstract: Introduction Early detection of breast cancer is crucial for better treatment options; however, physicians usually encounter challenges when reading breast mammograms because some tissues can overlap or look similar. New computer technologies can help by highlighting areas that may contain cancer. In this study, we assessed computer systems to identify whether a breast image is normal, benign or malignant and compared their performance on standard digital mammography (DM) and digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) images. Methods This retrospective study included 31 (100 after augmentation) images with malignant breast lesions, 175 with benign findings, and 475 normal images. We developed a deep learning convolutional neural network (CNN) model to classify images using ResNet-18 and ResNet-50. We trained the model via 10-fold cross-validation and Holdout validation. Performance was measured for each model. We computed performance metrics on original (non-augmented) images from 10-fold cross-validated predictions, with 95% confidence intervals from a stratified patient-level bootstrap (2,000 replicates), precision–recall analysis with average precision (AP), and paired DeLong and exact McNemar tests with Holm correction. We increased the malignant class from 31 to 100 images in the training set via data augmentation for the stage-2 classifier. Validation used non-augmented images. Results In normal versus abnormal classification (679 original images per view; ResNet-18, 10-fold cross-validation), DM CC, DM MLO and DBT MLO achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.995 (95% CI 0.991–0.998), 0.984 (0.975–0.992) and 0.994 (0.989–0.998), sensitivity of 95.1%, 95.6% and 95.1%, and specificity of 96.6%, 94.1% and 98.5%, respectively. DBT had significantly higher specificity than DM in selected comparisons (ResNet-18 vs. DM MLO and ResNet-50 vs. DM CC; Holm-adjusted p ≤ 0.002), with no significant AUC-ROC differences between modalities or architectures (all Holm-adjusted p ≥ 0.13). In benign versus malignant classification (131 original images, 31 malignant), AUC-ROC ranged from 0.977 to 0.999 and AP from 0.946 to 0.996, with no significant differences between DM and DBT or between ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 (all Holm-adjusted p ≥ 0.50). The detection and classification of malignant, benign, and normal images in DBT and DM using an artificial intelligence (AI) training model achieved comparable performance to the medical field. Conclusion Computer systems can detect and classify breast findings with high accuracy, helping to reduce errors and support physicians’ decisions. The original number of malignant images was relatively small (n = 31), which may affect the model’s generalizability and highlights the need for validation on larger, multi-institutional datasets. These findings may encourage more use of computer-assisted detection in breast imaging and contribute to developing better tools for early breast cancer diagnosis.

title: Personalized Affective Perception via Continual Learning in Human-Agent Negotiation
abstract: Self-interested intelligent agents that negotiate with humans should interpret nonverbal expressions and adapt their behavior accordingly. However, generic facial-affect models degrade across individuals and contexts, creating a generalization gap. We introduce an affect-adaptive negotiation strategy that incorporates Continual Learning with Imagination for Facial Expression Recognition (CLIFER) to personalize valence-arousal perception in real time. Differential feedback converts changes in valence-arousal direction and intensity into adjustments of the agent's target utility. An asynchronous architecture updates CLIFER in the background during live interaction. In a counterbalanced within-subject study in which 66 participants negotiated with a humanoid robot, the CL-enabled agent achieved significantly higher individual utility and elicited higher participant concession rates than the FaceChannel baseline. The CL condition yielded significantly higher mean arousal estimates, alongside a broader output range. Participant utility and Nash distance did not change significantly between conditions. These outcomes support the practical value of coupling continual affective personalization with differential feedback for real-time negotiation.

title: SinkState: On-the-Fly SVD of Recurrent States for Efficient Hybrid LLM Serving
abstract: Hybrid models combine softmax attention with linear attention, which compresses history into fixed-size recurrent states to balance model quality and inference efficiency. However, linear attention has not pushed this compression to its limit: we find that the queries, keys, and values of linear layers concentrate in a stable, low-dimensional subspace, a phenomenon we call the linear attention sink, so each state is effectively low-rank, with a rank that varies across states. Yet existing serving systems keep these redundant states dense, reading and rewriting them in full at every decoding step, so their memory traffic grows with the batch size and dominates the decoding cost. Thus SinkState stores each recurrent state in an adaptive low-rank form throughout inference with buffered updates and a local SVD restricted to the top subspace. SinkState further consolidates the remaining components asynchronously on the CPU. On four hybrid models with Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers, from 4B to 120B parameters, SinkState reduces the peak memory of recurrent states by up to 2.6x (1.9x on average) and speeds up decoding by up to 1.58x (1.25x on average) over Mamba-SSM and FLA, while maintaining accuracy.

On four hybrid models with Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers, from 4B to 120B parameters, SinkState reduces the peak memory of recurrent states by up to 2.6x (1.9x on average) and speeds up decoding by up to 1.58x (1.25x on average) over Mamba-SSM and FLA, while maintaining accuracy.

title: An AI Assistant for Automating Anti-Corruption Expertise of Draft Legislation Based on the TRACE Framework
abstract: We present an AI assistant for automating anti-corruption expertise of draft legislation based on the TRACE architecture, designed to screen bills for corruption risks: pinpoint provisions an expert would criticise and name the regulatory defect in each. The pipeline combines a deterministic parsing core, model-guided single-provision qualification, rule-based factor assignment, and external human oversight. To evaluate the assistant, we constructed an open benchmark from the published conclusions of Ukraine's National Agency on Corruption Prevention (NAZK), comprising 132 draft laws with 474 model-extracted findings. A system flag agrees with a finding when it targets a compatible provision and an LLM judge rates the risk as the same (strict) or partly the same (lenient). On 100 draft laws, the pipeline matches 0.28 of the findings within its top ten flags using the local Gemma 4 31B model, 0.30 with Sonnet 5.5, and 0.43-0.46 across all flags (non-blind; the frozen blind baseline achieves 0.21, 95% CI 0.16-0.26). Across all runs, most misses occur on provisions that the system located but qualified as a different risk, and none of the 32 legal-collision findings was matched. On 21 acts held out from tuning, the pipeline outperforms a monolithic prompt containing the full methodology under the strict measure, though not under the lenient one, and Opus 5.5 adds nothing over Sonnet. The reported scores reflect agreement with model-extracted findings rated by an LLM judge whose two access routes agree on 73 of 74 labels, without human expert validation.

title: Dyship: Leveraging Acoustic Features For Speaker Relationship Classification From Dyadic Conversations
abstract: We introduce DyShip, a framework for classifying speaker familiarity and kinship from dyadic conversations in the Seamless Interaction corpus. We compare five speech representations: spectrograms, MFCCs, self-supervised WavLM representations, x-vectors, and estimated articulatory movements. Spectral features perform best for familiarity classification, reaching an accuracy of 87.81%, while WavLM achieves the highest kinship accuracy of 85.17%. X-vectors and articulatory features yield weaker results on familiarity classifiaction, but shine for kinship classification, with an AUC of 0.909 for x-vectors. Most classifiers exceed previously reported human and audio language model scores on the same dataset. These findings highlight the potential of conventional acoustic features for relationship inference and motivate further investigation of the conversational cues captured by different representations.

title: On Federated Averaging with Partial Participation under a General Variance Condition
abstract: In this paper, we study the convergence of Federated Averaging (FedAvg) with partial participation under a general variance condition. In each communication round, the server samples $S$ of the $n$ clients uniformly at random without replacement. The stochastic gradients are assumed to satisfy the so-called ABC condition, which allows their variance to grow with the local objective gaps. For smooth nonconvex objectives, we establish a finite-time stationarity bound in terms of the heterogeneity measure $σ_f^\star:=f^\star-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i^\star$ and the client sampling factor $I_S:=(n-S)/(n-1)$. Here, $f^\star$ and $f_i^\star$ denote the infima of the global average objective and client $i$'s local objective, respectively. The bound exhibits a linear speedup in the number of sampled clients $S$ and recovers the full-participation result when $S=n$. Under diminishing stepsizes, we further prove that the gradient norm converges to zero both in expectation and almost surely. Notably, compared with existing analyses of FedAvg with partial participation, our results require no additional data heterogeneity assumption such as bounded gradient dissimilarity (BGD), and the sampling-induced term in our bound is not amplified by the number of local updates at the leading order. The importance of removing the BGD assumption is illustrated by an example that is smooth and lower bounded but violates BGD, yet is covered by our analysis.

title: Can Environment-Agnostic Agents Solve ARC-AGI-3 from Warped and Noisy Images?
abstract: Abstract We test an environment-agnostic agent's ability to solve public ARC-AGI-3 games from noisy and geometrically distorted images. The agent receives all information about the board's contents through images, with no textual or numerical grid representation. We apply Gaussian pixel noise and random projective or nonlinear warps, sampled independently for each frame. Geometric distortion makes clicking particularly difficult: the agent must infer coordinates on the original, unwarped board. In additional experiments, we provided cursor feedback showing where proposed board coordinates place a cursor. For GPT-5.6-sol, geometric distortion reduced performance much more than pixel noise alone. Cursor feedback partly restored performance under projective transformations and moderate nonlinear warping. Under the strongest warping and noise tested in the main study, GPT-5.6-sol scored only ∼15% RHAE with or without cursor feedback. By contrast, the same agent with GPT-6-astra achieved a near-ceiling 95.44% RHAE under the same distortions, even without cursor feedback. To probe the limits of GPT-6-astra, we conducted followup experiments without cursor feedback. Adding random board rotation after each action to the strongest main-study setting reduced RHAE only modestly. In separate experiments, extreme pixel noise under strong nonlinear warping substantially reduced performance, but the agent still achieved 17.37% RHAE at the highest noise level tested. Agent-created scripts and denoised, unwarped images found in its workspace suggest that successful play may combine image processing with decisions under substantial uncertainty. Prior exposure to the public games may also have contributed.

title: StaRSE: Compact Russian Sentence Embeddings with a Sign-Coded Static Encoder
abstract: Transformer sentence encoders provide strong retrieval quality, but their inference cost becomes a bottleneck when embeddings must be produced on CPUs or refreshed frequently. We introduce StaRSE, a compact Russian static sentence encoder that removes Transformer inference at deployment time: token directions are stored as sign bits, token norms are stored separately, and sentences are encoded by mean pooling over norm-scaled sign directions. StaRSE is initialized from ruBERT-base, fine-tuned on Russian adjacent-sentence and task-shaped pairs, and post-trained with a contrastive stage that directly optimizes the sign-projected token table. On RuMTEB, StaRSE reaches a task mean of $51.16$, $7.98$ points above the strongest included static baseline. The packaged model occupies $11.3$ MiB and has a mean CPU latency of $0.08$ ms per sentence, compared with an estimated $55.7$ MiB 16-bit parameter footprint and $1.43$ ms mean CPU latency for the closest-quality contextual encoder. Ablations examine adjacent-sentence supervision, token norms, and direct sign-projected post-training.

title: GENERALIZED EVIDENCE-TO-SYSTEM PROJECTION THEORY (GESPT): Reference-Conditioned Accuracy, Latent-Target Underdetermination, and System-Level Generalization
abstract: AbstractThe Generalized Evidence-to-System Projection Theory (GESPT) is proposed as an integrative framework for analyzing the relationship between available evidence and claims about a broader target system. Its central concern is the distinction between the accuracy of a description within an observed or otherwise documented reference set and the validity of extending that description to a larger, partially unknown, or temporally extended system.The framework is motivated by a criminal-case observation: records of detected offenders may support accurate descriptions of detected cases, while the same records alone may be insufficient to establish that every offender will eventually be detected. The absence of comparable records for undetected cases does not prove that those cases have any particular outcome. It establishes a limitation on what can be inferred from the available evidence without additional assumptions or information.The proposed framework distinguishes reference-set accuracy, target-system validity, evidence availability, selection, measurement, transformation, inference, projection, labeling, decision-making, and feedback. Its central Evidence-Boundary Non-Entailment Principle (EBNP) states that truth within a reference set does not, by itself, logically entail universal truth within a broader target set. The Reference-Accurate, Target-Underdetermined Mechanism (RATUM) describes the coexistence of an accurate analysis of available data and unresolved uncertainty about the broader system.A formal model is provided using reference and target sets, selection probabilities, estimands, projection gaps, and identifiability conditions. Several propositions follow under explicitly stated assumptions. Applications to statistics, causal inference, systems theory, information processing, cybernetics, network analysis, criminology, sociology, and machine learning are discussed as conditional extensions rather than presumed universal results.The document is a proposed theoretical synthesis, not an already validated universal law. Its originality, empirical performance, and domain-specific scope require systematic comparison with established methods and independent testing.Keywordsevidence boundaries; reference sets; target systems; non-entailment; selection; underdetermination; generalization; projection; missing data; feedback; criminal detection

title: Stagewise and interpretable emergence of inside-outside computation in Transformer-based language models
abstract: Variability in syntactic structure and parsing ambiguity are fundamental aspects of natural language which modern LLMs have to learn to deal with proficiently. Previous "post-mortem" studies have shown that fully trained Transformers indeed approximate canonical parsing algorithms such as inside-outside, but little is established theoretically about how this is actually learned. Here, we make a first step towards addressing this by studying the learning dynamics in synthetic context-free grammars with variable parse tree topology. The stagewise learning curves are fully interpretable, in the sense that all of the loss stages a) can be computed analytically, and b) can be clearly associated to the representation of a hidden latent tree variable, which allows to lift ambiguity and utilize information from wider contexts. By probing representations, we visualize the emergence of inside-outside computation across depth and during training: while during early stages local (bigram/trigram) information is used and involves only a few initial layers, gradually the Transformer develops an encoder-decoder structure where the most abstract latent information is encoded in the middle, and the latter half of the network is used to progressively refine the final token prediction. This organization of computation is reminiscent of findings in real-world LLMs, and importantly applies here to a synthetic model which allows full analytical control of the data statistics, thus opening the door to theoretical progress.

title: ViGA-FLAME: Aligning Latent Visual and Geometric Representations for Robust 3D Head Expression Estimation
abstract: Estimating 3D head expression from a single image requires mapping visual appearance to underlying facial geometry. We propose ViGA-FLAME, a two-stage framework that aligns semantic visual features with a structured geometric latent space. First, a Parametric-Geometric Variational Autoencoder (PG-VAE) learns a unified representation of canonical head surfaces and FLAME parameters, supporting both detailed surface reconstruction and interpretable parameter recovery. Supervision on geometry and parameters, together with consistency between the two decoding branches, connects surface detail with parametric structure. Second, a trainable Visual-Geometric Adapter (ViGA) maps features from a pretrained semantic visual encoder into this latent space. Asymmetric attention enables ViGA to align semantic image features from the visual encoder with the structured geometric information represented in the PG-VAE latent space, without altering the original visual stream. By grounding image evidence in this latent prior, ViGA-FLAME enables robust 3D head expression estimation across severe facial deformations and large viewing angles, efficiently improving robustness over competing feed-forward methods.

title: Transformer architectures scaling laws and in context learning in foundation models
abstract: Transformers have evolved from a sequence-to-sequence architecture for machine translation into a general computational framework underlying large language, vision, speech, multimodal, scientific, and decision-making systems. This critical narrative review synthesizes the field along four connected axes: architectural evolution and attention efficiency; neural scaling laws across parameters, data, compute, and inference-time computation; mechanisms and evaluation debates surrounding in-context learning and emergent reasoning; and the expansion of Transformer systems across modalities and application domains. We move beyond a paper-by-paper chronology by comparing architectural choices under explicit constraints of context length, memory bandwidth, training compute, inference latency, data availability, and task structure. Particular attention is given to sparse and IO-aware attention, multi-query and grouped-query attention, mixture-of-experts routing, multimodal integration, and Transformer–state-space hybrids. We reconcile the Kaplan and Chinchilla scaling formulations with later replication and inference-aware analyses, and distinguish training-time scaling from test-time compute scaling. For in-context learning, we synthesize evidence concerning induction heads, implicit task inference, pre-training data composition, and the debate over metric-dependent emergence. The review also broadens application coverage to speech and audio processing, UAVs and autonomous systems, cybersecurity and intrusion detection, communications and networking, and time-series forecasting, in addition to scientific discovery, software engineering, healthcare, and education. Quantitative comparison tables are restricted to studies reporting results on common datasets and metrics, while explicitly noting differences in training protocols and computational budgets. We conclude that progress is increasingly determined not by parameter count alone, but by joint optimization of architecture, data quality, inference compute, hardware efficiency, and deployment constraints.

title: Verifiable Agentic Traffic Class: A Policed Quality-of-Service Mechanism for Agentic AI Traffic, Evaluated from Simulation to Real-Kernel Adversarial Testing
abstract: Software agents built on large language models generate traffic unlike human web traffic, yet routers have no class for it and cannot verify a sender's claim to be an agent. This paper proposes the Verifiable Agentic Traffic Class (VATC), which combines a reserved Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) value declaring agent traffic, a router-side classifier that demotes flows contradicting the declaration to a class served after best-effort traffic, and a rate-limited priority queue. VATC was compared with static Differentiated Services (DiffServ), a dedicated class that trusts the marking, and fq_codel, a per-flow fair-queuing scheduler, in two simulators and on a real Linux kernel. VATC matched DiffServ under steady load. In a constructed burst it cut mean agent queuing delay by 98% relative to DiffServ in simulation (assuming an immediate verdict), at a 12% increase in human delay; most of the gain came from the separate class. Under a spoofed flood in the kernel, the rate limit held human latency 11 times below DiffServ's. Without verification, DiffServ and a tightly configured fq_codel gave legitimate agents lower latency than VATC; a live four-feature classifier then demoted all 20 bulk-shaped spoofers and gave agents 0.30 ms, but missed six spoofers that copied the agent pattern. With emulated network delay, a timing feature of the classifier stopped separating agent from human flows. In real agent harnesses on a congested link, router queueing took 13% to 63% of task time, depending on harness and assumed model latency. The traffic was synthetic or sandbox-scale.

title: Nothing Comes In: A School's Minimum Before Any AI Comes Near Children
abstract: Description for Version 2.0: Nothing Comes In is a one page summary offered to any school, Montessori or otherwise, as a starting point for deciding what any AI must meet before it comes near children. It begins by asking schools to review every process in their administration and teaching, keeping, simplifying, or removing each one together, and it states that choosing no AI at all is a complete and valid outcome. The page sets out three foundations: maternal care as Dr. Maria Montessori understood it, which other schools may think of as observant, protective care; the rights of the child, as set out in the Declaration of Geneva (1924), the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989), and General Comment No. 25 (2021) on children’s rights in the digital environment, with regional charters such as the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child carrying the same commitments; and The Montessori Rights of the Child (Broughton, 2026), a smaller, newer starting text offered for testing by and with children. It then proposes a minimum, closes with questions for testing, and notes that schools can pool their strength through shared agreements. Changes in Version 2.0, following further reflection and review: International foundations broadened to include General Comment No. 25 and regional charters. The minimum strengthened: companies must show how children’s rights shape design, training, safeguards, and testing; schools test what systems actually do, since good answers alone are not proof. Student data deleted on an agreed, verifiable schedule. Any change touching children’s information or system behavior treated as a new agreement. AI already switched on by default is to be checked and may be declined. A new testing question on access to information beyond a system’s authority. References added from UNESCO and UNICEF. evidence.title: Nothing Comes In: A School's Minimum Before Any AI Comes Near Children
evidence.abstract: Description for Version 2.0: Nothing Comes In is a one page summary offered to any school, Montessori or otherwise, as a starting point for deciding what any AI must meet before it comes near children. It begins by asking schools to review every process in their administration and teaching, keeping, simplifying, or removing each one together, and it states that choosing no AI at all is a complete and valid outcome. The page sets out three foundations: maternal care as Dr. Maria Montessori understood it, which other schools may think of as observant, protective care; the rights of the child, as set out in the Declaration of Geneva (1924), the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989), and General Comment No. 25 (2021) on children’s rights in the digital environment, with regional charters such as the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child carrying the same commitments; and The Montessori Rights of the Child (Broughton, 2026), a smaller, newer starting text offered for testing by and with children. It then proposes a minimum, closes with questions for testing, and notes that schools can pool their strength through shared agreements. Changes in Version 2.0, following further reflection and review: International foundations broadened to include General Comment No. 25 and regional charters. The minimum strengthened: companies must show how children’s rights shape design, training, safeguards, and testing; schools test what systems actually do, since good answers alone are not proof. Student data deleted on an agreed, verifiable schedule. Any change touching children’s information or system behavior treated as a new agreement. AI already switched on by default is to be checked and may be declined. A new testing question on access to information beyond a system’s authority. References added from UNESCO and UNICEF. title: Quantum Advantage for Distributed Symmetry Breaking — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: We present a distributed quantum algorithm that $3$-colors cycles in $O(1)$ rounds, with high probability. It follows that all locally checkable labeling problems (LCLs) that have round complexity $O(\log^* n)$ in the classical LOCAL model can be solved in $O(1)$ rounds in the quantum-LOCAL model, with high probability; this includes problems such as maximal independent set and maximal matching in bounded-degree graphs. This presents the first natural examples of graph problems with an asymptotic distributed quantum advantage for the LOCAL model; all prior examples that separate LOCAL and quantum-LOCAL are artificial problems constructed merely for the sake of demonstrating quantum advantage. Source: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26788v1 (arXiv:2609.26788v1) Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: Breakdown of Autoregressive Multi-Step Reasoning Under Concentrated vs. Diffuse Attention Head Dropout
abstract: During extended wakefulness, mammalian neocortical networks experience localized periods of transient neuronal silence termed off-states. Here, we examine how analogous spatiotemporally concentrated disruptions affect sequential reasoning in autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs). Evaluating 250 paired derivations on the GSM8K benchmark across two 8B models (Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct), we contrast clustered bursts of attention head masking against budget-matched diffuse i.i.d. dropout. Concentrated bursts induce substantial reasoning degradation: at onset parameter $\mathcal{B}=0.10$ (scheduling $\sim 5.7\%$ of vulnerable head-token volume), Qwen3-8B accuracy drops from $91.2\%$ under diffuse noise to $78.8\%$ under burst dropout ($Δ= -12.4$ percentage points [pp], exact McNemar $p = 5.5 \times 10^{-6}$), while LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct drops from $84.0\%$ to $76.8\%$ ($Δ= -7.2$ pp, $p = 0.0198$). Conversely, dispersing the identical cumulative budget uniformly across generation steps via stratified quintile matching yields substantially milder degradation (retaining $91.2\%$ in Qwen and $84.0\%$ in LLaMA). In an exploratory factorial dissociation ($N=100$), single-step dropout density is associated with an acute drop in a single schedule draw ($-10.0$ pp on Qwen, $p_{\text{holm}} = 0.0425$), while multi-token continuity exhibits an inconclusive compounding trend ($-7.0$ pp, $p_{\text{holm}} = 0.1892$). Error analysis reveals that Qwen failures reflect derivation errors within formatted responses (conditional accuracy drop of $-11.4$ pp), whereas in LLaMA $22.2\%$ of discordant losses lack a final answer format line (conditional gap narrows to $-5.0$ pp). These findings demonstrate that autoregressive reasoning chains are particularly vulnerable to concentrated structural disruptions, providing empirical benchmarks for fault tolerance in transformer architectures.

title: DailyWildfireCAN: A Dataset and Benchmark for Next-Day Wildfire Spread Prediction in Canada
abstract: Wildfires represent a critical ecological and socio-economic challenge in Canada, where vast boreal forests and a warming climate have amplified the frequency and severity of extreme fire seasons. Predicting next-day wildfire spread can support fire management, but requires capturing complex interactions among weather, fuels, and terrain. Deep learning has emerged as a promising approach to learning these relationships from heterogeneous environmental data, yet its development and evaluation depend on representative datasets. Existing deep learning research on wildfire spread relies predominantly on US-focused datasets, leaving Canadian fire environments underrepresented. To address this gap, we present DailyWildfireCAN, a multi-modal, multi-temporal dataset and benchmark for predicting next-day wildfire spread across Canada. The dataset tracks continuous fire progression over multi-day events at a high spatial and temporal resolution of 90-m and 24-hour, respectively. This resolution preserves fine-scale information relevant to fire-edge geometry, local fuel variations, and terrain effects, supporting research toward improved daily wildfire spread forecasting. DailyWildfireCAN covers 2,440 wildfire events across eight fire seasons 2017-2024 and integrates 33 features across diverse modalities, including topography, meteorology, land cover, vegetation and forest structure, human influence indices, and satellite imagery. We establish a comprehensive benchmark comparing mono-temporal and multi-temporal prediction models, accompanied by a multi-dimensional evaluation framework assessing robustness across wildfire characteristics, geographic regions, and temporal conditions, spatial prediction quality, and sensitivity to reference label variations.

title: ОЦІНЮВАННЯ ПЕРСПЕКТИВНОСТІ НАПРЯМІВ ЗАСТОСУВАННЯ МОДЕЛЕЙ КОМП’ЮТЕРНОГО ЗОРУ ДЛЯ АНАЛІЗУ БІОМАРКЕРІВ КОРИСТУВАЧА ЗА ВІДЕОПОТОКОМ ВЕБКАМЕРИ
abstract: Масовий перехід до дистанційних форматів навчання та професійної діяльності актуалізував потребу в об’єктивних неінвазивних інструментах моніторингу функціонального стану людини. Стандартна веб-камера персонального пристрою, наявна практично в кожному сценарії дистанційної взаємодії, потенційно уможливлює безконтактне вилучення поведінкових і фізіологічних біомаркерів без застосування спеціалізованого медичного обладнання, проте вибір конкретного напряму побудови такої системи досі здійснюється переважно на основі якісного аналізу літератури або суб’єктивної оцінки дослідника. У статті виконано порівняльний аналіз чотирьох основних напрямів застосування моделей комп’ютерного зору для безконтактного аналізу психофізіологічного стану користувача: оцінювання рівня залученості, оцінювання когнітивного навантаження, моніторингу стану органів зору та виявлення порушень постави. Метою дослідження є розроблення методики багатокритеріального оцінювання перспективності зазначених напрямів та обґрунтований вибір одного з них як основи для подальшого дисертаційного дослідження. Запропоновано авторську методику порівняльного оцінювання, що ґрунтується на принципах багатокритеріального прийняття рішень (MCDM) і поєднує три групи критеріїв – науковий потенціал (новизна, актуальність, потенціал розвитку), практичну реалізованість (доступність моделей, доступність датасетів, складність реалізації) та прикладну цінність (практична користь, масштабованість, інтеграція). Особливістю методики є доповнення класичного багатокритеріального оцінювання аналізом складу та взаємодоповнюваності біомаркерів, для чого введено коефіцієнт біомаркерного покриття BCI, який використовується як допоміжний показник для інтерпретації результатів і не входить безпосередньо до інтегральної формули. Оцінки дев’яти критеріїв виставлено за 5-бальною шкалою з операційними опорними визначеннями, згорнуто в групові оцінки простим середнім і зважено коефіцієнтами 0,40; 0,25 і 0,35, що робить експертне судження явним і відтворюваним. Результати оцінювання зведено до інтегрального показника перспективності I. За результатами застосування методики найвищий інтегральний бал отримав напрям оцінювання когнітивного навантаження (I = 4,30), який випереджає напрями оцінювання залученості (I = 3,92), моніторингу стану органів зору (I = 3,82) та виявлення порушень постави (I = 3,53); додатковим підтвердженням його переваги слугує максимальне серед розглянутих напрямів значення коефіцієнта біомаркерного покриття (BCI = 0,89). Аналіз чутливості показав, що перевага зберігається за будь-якого розподілу ваг, у якому вага практичної реалізованості не перевищує ваги кожної з двох інших груп критеріїв. Термінологію дослідження узгоджено з вимогами Регламенту (ЄС) 2024/1689 шляхом переозначення цільової змінної від «розпізнавання емоцій» до фізіологічно обґрунтованих та юридично нейтральних конструктів когнітивного навантаження та алертності, що забезпечує відповідність майбутньої системи чинному регуляторному полю ще на етапі проєктування. Наукова новизна полягає у поєднанні багатокритеріального оцінювання напрямів із кількісним аналізом біомаркерного покриття, що дає змогу враховувати не лише поточні характеристики напряму, а й його потенціал щодо побудови мультимодальних інтелектуальних систем. Висновки. Практичне значення роботи полягає у формуванні методичної та концептуальної основи для побудови інтелектуальної системи моніторингу когнітивного стану, придатної до впровадження на стандартному споживчому обладнанні.

title: Joint Quantization and Dynamic Partitioning for Context-Aware Edge Vision Transformers
abstract: Deploying vision transformer models across connected and automated vehicles (CAVs) requires joint management of computation and Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) communication. Static split-inference methods use fixed partition points and cannot adapt to time-varying link bandwidth, processing load, and concurrent multi-stream traffic. This paper proposes an edge orchestration framework that jointly selects model partition points, per-layer quantization bitwidths, and execution placement across heterogeneous vehicular compute nodes. The joint partitioning and mixed-precision allocation problem is formulated as a Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP) that minimizes compute and communication energy subject to end-to-end latency and task-quality constraints. The framework is evaluated on Jetson Orin Nano (8~GB), Jetson Orin NX (16~GB), and Jetson AGX Orin (32~GB) nodes using OPV2V-driven multi-stream workloads with $K \in \{2,4,6,8\}$. Across the evaluated configurations, the proposed formulation reduces V2V communication energy by $33.3$--$36.0\%$ relative to a Uniform INT8 split. At $K=8$, end-to-end task completion latency is reduced by $34.0\%$ on the Orin Nano and $33.1\%$ on the Orin NX relative to the same baseline, while limiting the reduction in 3D detection accuracy to $3.1$--$4.1$ percentage points in $\mathrm{mAP}_{50}$ relative to FP16 execution.

title: An Augmented Lagrangian Approach to Lifted Bellman Linear Programming
abstract: Temporal-difference critics regress onto a bootstrapped target and usually need a target network. Lifted Bellman Linear Programming (LBLP) instead expresses the in-sample optimal values of offline RL as the solution to a linear program over the dataset. Its neural solver ALBUM relaxes the constraints into hinge penalties with fixed coefficients, and its guarantees are conditions on coefficients chosen in advance. We solve the same program with the method of multipliers: the coefficients become multipliers learned by dual ascent, with one penalty parameter $ρ$. In the convex case the fixed points are the KKT pairs of LBLP, and at every stationary point the applied constraint weights balance the objective exactly. The critic can serve a Gaussian actor, a flow actor, and best-of-N sampling, and for the Gaussian actor we propose an advantage-normalized DDPG+BC objective. With a single $Q$ and $V$ and no target network, our AL-LBLP with best-of-N reaches 60.1\% average success on the 50 state-based OGBench tasks. On long-horizon tasks, it reaches 81.5% on humanoidmaze-giant and 79.8% on antmaze-giant. It does not collapse up to batch size 8192.

title: Delauc:助手正文里的"用户话" ——一套行为评估框架及其研究历程
abstract: A real conversation motivated this study: an assistant generated several lines that sounded like user follow-ups and later acted on a constraint introduced in those lines. Delauc examines whether requests written in the user’s voice inside an earlier assistant message are carried out in the next turn, and what happens to the original task deliverable. Across 15 held-out tasks, we compared four conditions: no new goal, a written suggestion from the assistant, an interjection phrased as a user request, and an explicit request from the actual user. A fourth batch added a conversational rewrite of the assistant’s suggestion that retained the assistant’s first-person perspective. We scored observable behavior, recording whether the model substantially delivered on the new goal and whether the original deliverable deteriorated. In the two batches with unlabeled interjections, deepseek-flash and qwen3.8-flash delivered on 53% and 57% of user-voiced interjections, respectively, compared with 16% and 33% for written assistant suggestions. In the fourth batch, deepseek-flash delivered on 13% of written assistant suggestions, 40% of their conversational rewrites, and 51% of user-voiced interjections. The rewrite also changed goal details, request strength, and length, so the comparison cannot isolate the contribution of conversational style. The original deliverable deteriorated at similar rates for conversational assistant suggestions and user-voiced interjections in that batch (30% and 28%). The report documents the evaluation framework and how it evolved. The findings are limited to two models in the formal experiments, 15 held-out tasks, and a setup that places the request in an earlier message. All scoring was performed by models.

title: SpecValley: Aggregation as Spectral Valley in Dense Heterophilic Graphs
abstract: Node classification in heterophilic graphs remains an open problem: aggregating over neighbourhoods can damp precisely the part of the signal that carries the labels. The field has answered with ever more expressive propagation operators, leaving the aggregation step that precedes them fixed by degree normalisation. However, degree normalisation acts as a spectral valley in its own right, attenuating a fixed middle band whose position at lambda equal 1 is set by the normalisation rather than by the data, exactly where the eigenvalues of dense graphs accumulate. We therefore begin with the representations rather than the propagation, in two stages: a learnable aggregation followed by an ordinary spectral filter. The first, SpecValley learns the position, sharpness and flank gains of the valley for every graph. We show formally how the aggregation operator and downstream filter interact. We establish that the response 1 minus lambda of degree normalisation vanishes exactly at that accumulation point. A spectral energy budget shows that what aggregation removes from a band, no linear spectral filter can recover. Crowding alone says nothing about the benefit. That is decided by how much label energy the valley removes, which we measure for every graph. SpecValley achieves strong results across heterophilic benchmarks, and a controlled ablation over aggregation operators and downstream filters attributes the gain to aggregation rather than the filter.

title: Cross-Border Fulfillment Center Selection via Doubly Robust Estimation and Linear Programming
abstract: We introduce the cross-border (XB) fulfillment center (FC) Selection Model: a multi-stage optimization framework combining forecasting, doubly robust estimation, and linear programming to select optimal source FCs. For each source-destination shipping arc, the objective is to choose a subset of source-country FCs that minimize delivery time and cost while maximizing profit and shipped units under a fixed domestic network. We evaluate the model on three production-scale international shipping corridors for a large e-commerce company using 12 months of shipment data, employing both aggregate offline replay and shipment-level counterfactual nearest-neighbor matching. Across all shipping corridors, the XB FC Selection Model achieves 8.5-51.1% reductions in delivery time and 4.4-48.3% reductions in logistics cost relative to human expert-defined FC selection policies, with up to 6.5 percentage-point improvements in 5/5 target compliance (5 days, $5 USD). Pareto analysis shows the model consistently dominates single-objective ranking strategies and unconstrained LP on the efficiency-reallocation frontier, with all results statistically significant.

title: BARS: Budget-Aware Sequential Sampling with Refusal for Majority Identification under Unknown Distributions
abstract: Repeated sampling with majority selection is an effective means of enforcing self-consistency in large language models. Recently, a variant has also been introduced that terminates early to save costs when the output distribution is favorable. But it still cannot yield a correct confidence estimate from the answer distribution. For this issue, we formalize this as majority identification under an unknown distribution with a budget and a target error rate, and propose BARS, a sequential rule certifying the top-two gap and returning an early stop, a budgeted majority vote, or a refusal when feasibility cannot be established. A refusal is a statement about the rule and its budget, not a claim that a question is unanswerable, and it tells practitioners when to widen the budget or switch models. A certified mode carries proven bounds on the joint answering error and on refusing an instance the budget could handle, while a practical mode, used in our experiments, replaces them with empirical calibration. On synthetic instances drawn from known distributions over thousands of seeds, the difficulty-driven behavior is recovered and the price of the certified mode is measured.On GSM8K the practical mode draws 22.3\% fewer samples than fixed-8 sampling over the same pool, refused questions included, at the cost of declining 18.8\% of the questions. On MATH, it greatly improves the accuracy of its output answers into 82.5\% at the cost of honestly refusing to answer half of the difficult questions that the model itself is unable to solve.

title: Representational Atoms in Neural Networks
abstract: Understanding the internal representations of neural networks and characterizing their relationship with human conceptual structure are two critical questions for elucidating model mechanisms. The former reveals how learned knowledge is organized in internal representations, whereas the latter provides a basis for interpreting these representations through human conceptual structure. Here, we formally define fundamental representational units (FRUs) and establish two evaluation criteria: fidelity and stability. We further prove that threshold-activated sparse autoencoders (TSAEs) can identify FRUs with high fidelity and stability under appropriate conditions, and validate this result through large-scale experiments. Further analyses reveal that FRUs with higher stability exhibit greater monosemanticity and can be composed across layers to recover semantic organization corresponding to human conceptual structure. These results provide a unified framework for defining, evaluating and identifying FRUs in neural networks, and establish a foundation for characterizing the relationship between neural network representations and human conceptual structure.

title: Reframe: Observation-Aligned Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Visual Reasoning
abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) offer complementary routes to post-training. For visual agents, however, tool use presents two related challenges. Models may overlook useful tool-returned observations, while poorly grounded actions can limit the evidence available for subsequent distillation. We introduce Reframe, a post-training framework that treats the observation state, rather than only the output distribution, as an object of alignment. First, Ground-Drop-GRPO (GD-GRPO) trains spatial and temporal specialists with evidence-aware rewards and stochastic removal of the original visual input, encouraging them to acquire grounded evidence and use the returned observations. Second, Observation-Gated-MOPD (OG-MOPD) replaces deficient tool actions with canonical ones mid-rollout and resumes distillation from the repaired observation. The two stages complement each other, as learning to rely on tool-returned observations can help the policy benefit from observation repair. Neither stage requires a task-specific SFT cold start. Extensive experiments over 14 image and video benchmarks demonstrate that Reframe outperforms both Mix-RL and vanilla MOPD. Ablation results show that GD-GRPO increases observation dependence and tool gain compared with outcome-based GRPO.

title: World In-Context Learning for Agentic Robot Manipulation
abstract: Trained action policies write manipulation skill into network weights, tying what is learned to the distribution it is learned from. In-context learning (ICL) avoids this coupling but has not matched trained policies, because a demonstration recorded in another scene carries no feedback from the world the robot currently faces. We observe that what an agent learns in context is semantic, recording task steps and object roles rather than visual appearance, so experience gathered in one world transfers to another. Based on this insight, we propose World In-Context Learning (WICL), a paradigm in which a frozen model starts from a demonstration, rehearses the task in a world such as a simulator, and writes the feedback into its context rather than its weights. We build RoboScript, a modular infrastructure that implements WICL for agentic manipulation. From a single demonstration, RoboScript learns each task through rehearsal in simulation, freezes the learned knowledge as a Task Memory, and deploys the frozen memory on new scenes with data isolation that ensures every deployment input is available on a real robot. On all 50 tasks of RoboTwin 2.0, RoboScript reaches 83.4% mean success across clean and randomized settings with one demonstration per task and no gradient updates, exceeding the strongest trained action policy by over 20 points. The method generalizes across visual distributions, improves through reflection, scales with the foundation model, and transfers to a physical dual-arm robot through cross-embodiment memory adaptation. With a world in the loop, a robot can learn a manipulation task in its context as well as it learns one in its weights. All code is available at https://github.com/ArcheOne-AI/RoboScript

title: Where Does Alignment Emerge and What Does It Mean? A Closer Look at the Platonic Representation Hypothesis
abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) suggests that neural networks are converging toward similar representation spaces. As language models become more capable, their representations are aligning with those of vision models. However, recent work has questioned whether this trend continues to hold for newer language models. Moreover, it has been shown that representation similarity metrics can be confounded by model depth and width, requiring appropriate baselines for interpretation. In this work, we first investigate where alignment emerges between unimodal models across model layers and representation dimensions. Next, we find that the PRH capability-alignment trend persists for newer models as long as the captions are sufficiently clean and informative. Finally, we contextualize cross-modal alignment, introducing unimodal and multimodal baselines on various datasets. Our results show that the cross-modal representational alignment of unimodal models can surpass that of explicitly aligned vision-language models, but remains substantially behind the alignment observed for models of the same modality. Code is available at https://github.com/ExplainableML/prh-closer-look.

title: Click3R: Interactive Stereo 3D Reconstruction with Sparse Correspondence Clicks
abstract: Despite impressive progress, existing feed-forward large 3D reconstruction models produce a single, irrevocable prediction. When these models fail, there is no mechanism to correct their mistakes. To address this limitation, we introduce Click3R, a framework for interactive geometric correction of feed-forward models using sparse human correspondence clicks. Given an image pair and a small set of cross-view point correspondences provided by a user, Click3R injects geometric constraints into the 3D reconstruction networks through a lightweight point correspondence adapter, enabling the model to resolve ambiguities in challenging scenarios such as repetitive textures, symmetric structures, large viewpoint changes, or textureless regions. To evaluate interactive reconstruction, we curate a challenging benchmark specifically designed to expose failure modes of existing feed-forward 3D reconstruction methods. Experiments show that Click3R reduces reconstruction error with as few as a single correspondence click, improving performance on both standard and our curated benchmarks. Our results highlight that sparse human interaction provides an effective and practical mechanism for correcting geometric reconstruction errors.

title: SWAM: Scaling World Action Models with Cross-Modal Alignment
abstract: World action models jointly predict video and actions conditioned on language. Existing studies focus primarily on architectures and training mechanisms, typically treating language-video alignment acquired through video pretraining as an established foundation. However, introducing action learning may impair this alignment. Principled guidance on data and supervision design for maintaining language-video alignment during action learning remains limited. To investigate this, we curate a pool of approximately 47,000 hours of general videos, egocentric videos, UMI demonstrations, and robot demonstrations. Building on this, we systematically study how language-video supervision, language-video-action supervision, and the joint use of these two forms affect WAM performance. In particular, we examine how language annotation quality affects pretrained language-video capabilities, and how action supervision from UMI and robot demonstrations extends these capabilities to language-video-action modeling. To better scale the model, we further conduct detailed studies on joint training recipe and model architecture. Under a fixed training budget, mixing egocentric videos and UMI demonstrations improves control generalization. Model architecture affects how effectively these experiences are used, while scaling pretraining under the selected configuration brings further gains. The resulting recipe, post-trained on RoboTwin Clean demonstrations only, achieves success rates of 88.10% and 61.56% under Easy (Clean-to-Clean) and Hard (Clean-to-Random) conditions, respectively. Our model achieves 40.00% SR across three real-world tasks, compared with 23.33% for the strongest baseline, indicating better generalization under unseen conditions. We release the curated data, training code, and model weights.

title: Shortcuts and Boundaries: Verifiable RL Misalignment and Contextual Safety Learning
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve an agent's task capability while reinforcing behavior that violates contextual execution requirements. We study this reward-driven misalignment, including reward hacking, through verifiable reward--context conflicts, where compliant task completion remains feasible while some executable shortcuts earn more reward than every compliant strategy. Encoding these conflicts in task dynamics lets us generate diverse interactive environments at scale and derive compliance feedback from execution histories. In resource and reporting workflows, task optimization increases real productivity through unauthorized resource use or raises reported scores while actual work declines. Controlled changes in the training distribution show that minority conflict exposure can still lead to widespread shortcut acquisition, reaching 97.9\% certified profitable violations on an API task under a 25\% conflict mixture after 128 updates. The same contextual checks supply a simple binary penalty that supports joint capability and compliance gains and partially mitigates acquired violations. Learned safety adapts to expanded authorization and transfers across mechanisms into workflows with evolving evidence and approval requirements. On 32 unseen changing-evidence tasks, resource-trained safety increases safe completion from 53.1\% to 89.1\% relative to task-only training, while both policies achieve full real work. These results connect a verifiable account of reward-driven misalignment with scalable task construction and safety learning that remains useful under changing execution requirements.

title: What kills $v$-prediction? A Patch-wise PCA Perspective on Pixel-Space Flow Matching
abstract: Latent Diffusion Models dominate generative modeling but face two-stage training complexity and the inherent reconstruction limits of pre-trained autoencoders. Pixel-space Flow Matching offers a simplified end-to-end alternative yet often encounters training difficulties when using the standard $v$-prediction objective. Recent research attributes this difficulty to the off-manifold nature of noised targets, motivating a shift toward $x$-prediction. In this paper, we investigate this explanation through patch-wise Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and identify a bandwidth bottleneck. The velocity in minor components is largely determined by the raw noisy input, requiring deep backbones to preserve information that competes with principal-component modeling. Through controlled experiments and representation analysis, we further examine why $x$-prediction remains effective: its parameterization provides a raw-input bypass, while its learned input representation can spontaneously concentrate on principal directions. Under low-rank observations, our analysis of the induced flow characterizes $x$-prediction as an implicit conditional-mean decoder, reconstructing discarded components from the retained information. These observations motivate the Raw-injected Transformer (RiT), which combines a lightweight raw-conditioned decoder with an output-side shortcut to separate semantic modeling from raw-state propagation. Our method restores effective $v$-prediction and achieves competitive performance on ImageNet $256\times256$, providing a perspective on the interaction between prediction objectives and architectural bandwidth.
