title: SkillDuet: Co-Evolving Models and Skills through Response Feedback
abstract: During reinforcement learning, experience can be both internalized in LLM parameters and retained externally as reusable textual skills. Parameter updates alter the model's behavior and the interaction experience from which new skills are extracted. These skills, in turn, guide the model's subsequent interactions and parameter updates. As the model's capabilities evolve, previously beneficial skills may become redundant or detrimental. We present SkillDuet, a framework that coordinates parameter updates and skill evolution through model response feedback. Skills extracted from on-policy trajectories guide parameter updates through OPD at every step. A response-based score, Strength, ranks candidate skills by the magnitude of the shift they induce in the current model's responses, and the highest-scoring skills are periodically consolidated into a persistent global skill set (Global). The updated model and Global jointly guide subsequent interactions, generating experience for further parameter and skill updates. With Qwen3-4B, SkillDuet achieves success rates of 98.57% on ALFWorld and 92.97% on WebShop, exceeding the matched SEED-API baseline by 2.86 and 5.47 percentage points, respectively. Ablations show that response-based skill selection and Global consolidation improve task performance. Further experiments show that the benefits of retained skills depend on both their content and their compatibility with the model. SkillDuet provides a concrete mechanism for model-skill co-evolution and skill-level recursive self-improvement.

title: PkgScanArena: Benchmarking LLM-Based Package Scanners against Indirect Prompt Injection
abstract: Open-source package ecosystems such as PyPI and npm remain persistent targets for malicious campaigns. These campaigns have outgrown signature-based triage, so recent work has turned to large language models (LLMs) that scan package content and return a verdict, which lets the analysis consume attacker-controlled text. In 2026, the Hades campaign on PyPI carried a prompt injection written to hijack the scanner’s instructions and coerce a clean verdict. Indirect prompt injection is well studied, but its reach into automated package-security analysis remains unmeasured. We therefore ask a broader question. How reliable are LLM-based package scanners when the package itself is written to manipulate the analysis? We present PkgScanArena, a benchmark that pairs a vetted dataset of 2,000 malicious and 1,000 benign npm and PyPI packages with a taxonomy of 11 techniques and 3 injection channels across three attacker goals, namely evasion, denial, and sabotage. An AST-guided pipeline injects these prompts into real packages, and we evaluate 25 open-weight and proprietary model configurations together with two deployed scanners. Our benchmark inverts the expected threat. Evasion proves largely unattainable, at or below 0.6% for nine of ten cloud models. Exposure instead shifts to the opposite direction: benign accuracy degrades for all but two of the 25 backends, sabotage reaches 31.1%, and denial reaches 19.6% on the most safety-aligned model. The two deployed scanners inherit both weaknesses. The exposure lies not in coercing a scanner to miss malicious code, but in coercing it to condemn benign code.

title: Library of Hands: Fix the Hands, Not the World Model
abstract: A world model predicts how a scene changes after an action, and a planner uses it to search for actions that reach a goal. If the camera moves or the controller changes, the same command moves the robot differently: when its commands are turned by 90 degrees, a frozen planner with the LeWM world model that succeeds in 77.5% of episodes succeeds in only 7.8%. Current fixes retrain the model, need training data, or forget a set-up when it returns. We propose Library of Hands (LoH), a training-free method that keeps the world model frozen and corrects only the map from commands to applied actions, which we call the hand. LoH reads the hand through the frozen model, with no extra sensor: it finds the action that best explains the change between two camera images (a reading). It stores every hand it identifies, so a returning set-up is recognised rather than re-learnt. In closed-loop tests, LoH more than doubles success on three simulated tasks, from 28.6% to 62.3%, and loses only 0.6 percentage points when nothing changes. It also works, unchanged, with two other world models and on two of three models pretrained on real robot data, and its gain grows with the quality of its readings.

title: MIRIX-2.0: Multi-Agent Memory System
abstract: Long-term memory lets LLM agents personalize, stay consistent, and reuse what worked before. Parametric memories need training, consolidation can lose details for good, and keeping every record leaves a growing store to search. We present MIRIX-2.0, a multi-agent memory system designed to be practical, accurate, and efficient at once. It is the most accurate of the compared systems on four of five QA benchmarks. It reaches 91.4% on LoCoMo and 72.6% on LongMemEval-S, where it leads the strongest baseline by 14.3 points, and with AutoDream disabled it gains 31.0 and 22.0 points over HyperMem on single-hop and multi-hop document QA. As procedural memory, it yields the highest mean success among the compared memory methods on ALFWorld and WebShop and reaches 49.2% on MetaClaw-Bench, against 44.0% for MetaClaw's skill library. Six typed memory agents keep complete records as the system of record, and a provenance hypergraph indexes episodic and semantic records with n-ary frames that cite their rows. Retrieval runs under explicit budgets, so the evidence a question inspects does not grow with the history. AutoDream merges duplicate anchors outside the write path without rewriting any record, and it distills task sessions into skills. With AutoDream disabled, MIRIX-2.0 answers faster than HyperMem on all five timed benchmarks. It needs no fine-tuning, runs with closed and open models, and its code is public.

title: Detecting Spurious Periodic Generalization in Neural Networks PGVP
abstract: Modern neural networks often achieve near-perfect performance within the training distribution while failing catastrophically under structured distributional shifts. This failure mode is especially prevalent in periodic and cyclic learning tasks, where models may interpolate locally without learning the underlying generative structure. This work introduces the Periodic Generalization Verification Protocol (PGVP), a model-agnostic diagnostic framework designed to distinguish true periodic generalization from spurious in-domain curve fitting. PGVP evaluates trained models under controlled periodic out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts and quantifies the resulting Periodic Generalization Gap using standard regression metrics. Through controlled evaluations, we show that standard multilayer perceptrons frequently exhibit catastrophic periodic OOD failure despite near-perfect in-domain accuracy, while models with explicit periodic inductive bias generalize reliably. The protocol provides a structural validation layer that complements standard train/validation pipelines. PGVP is intended for pre-deployment model validation in applications involving time-series forecasting, signal processing, cyclic feature modeling, and physics-informed learning. Note: Figures included in this work are illustrative and intended to visualize typical behaviors targeted by the PGVP protocol rather than report specific experimental runs. The PGVP framework constitutes original intellectual work by the author. Specific decision thresholds and implementation details are intentionally omitted to preserve proprietary methodology.

title: VLA Adaptation with Real and Simulated Data: A Case Study on Robotic Chess
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are trained as general-purpose foundation models for robot learning, and require fine-tuning for each downstream task and robot. This raises practical questions such as how much data and training updates are needed, how checkpoints should be selected, and whether simulation can be leveraged to alleviate the cost of real data collection. We study these questions on a task that requires both precise manipulation and spatial understanding of the scene. In this task, an SO-101 arm moves a chess king between two squares that are given only by their names, such as e4 and a5. We fine-tune $π_{0.5}$ with various dataset sizes and update budgets, using teleoperated demonstrations as well as simulated demonstrations from a randomized scripted expert that imitates the variability of human demonstrations. In simulation, the success rate scales with both data and updates. Importantly, we find that a short learning-rate cool-down adds up to 31 points and is necessary for comparing checkpoints, and that validation loss and action error are unreliable for model selection. On the real arm, we fine-tune on up to 256 teleoperated demonstrations and evaluate ten policies in 25 trials each. Partial results indicate that pretraining on the simulated demonstrations helps substantially, most clearly when real data is scarce. We also present a negative result, in which training on the policy's own rollouts with filtered behavior cloning, RECAP-style advantage conditioning, corrections from an automatic coach, or residual reinforcement learning did not yield a measurable improvement over plain behavior cloning in our setting. We release the simulator, the expert and the real demonstrations.

title: Infrathon: Benchmarking Language Agents for Real-World, Long-Horizon AI Infra Optimization
abstract: In this work, we study whether frontier agent can continually improve real-world AI infrastructure over long horizons. We introduce Infrathon, a benchmark of diverse, long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks across different levels. We evaluate six models across 150 runs with 24-hour budgets, totaling over 10,000 GPU-hours. Our results show that model rankings vary with the evaluation horizon, while 135 of the 150 runs achieve further improvements during the second half of their budgets. These findings indicate that shorter evaluations can overlook both optimization gains and changes in relative model performance. We also find agents can discover solutions that outperform human-designed baselines: Claude Opus 5.5 increases the mean KV-cache compression ratio from 6.82% with the human-designed Quant-VideoGen codec to 19.86%. Analysis of agent trajectories identifies task violations, unreliable testing, and premature completion as barriers to sustained improvement. Together, Our Infrathon framework provide resources for constructing long-horizon tasks, evaluating frontier agents, and discovering good infrastructure solutions.

evidence.title: Infrathon: Benchmarking Language Agents for Real-World, Long-Horizon AI Infra Optimization
evidence.abstract: In this work, we study whether frontier agent can continually improve real-world AI infrastructure over long horizons. We introduce Infrathon, a benchmark of diverse, long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks across different levels. We evaluate six models across 150 runs with 24-hour budgets, totaling over 10,000 GPU-hours. Our results show that model rankings vary with the evaluation horizon, while 135 of the 150 runs achieve further improvements during the second half of their budgets. These findings indicate that shorter evaluations can overlook both optimization gains and changes in relative model performance. We also find agents can discover solutions that outperform human-designed baselines: Claude Opus 5.5 increases the mean KV-cache compression ratio from 6.82% with the human-designed Quant-VideoGen codec to 19.86%. Analysis of agent trajectories identifies task violations, unreliable testing, and premature completion as barriers to sustained improvement. Together, Our Infrathon framework provide resources for constructing long-horizon tasks, evaluating frontier agents, and discovering good infrastructure solutions.

title: Interpretability Is Not Model-Specific
abstract: Interpretability tools are usually built for one model at a time: a refusal direction, a truthfulness probe, or a steering vector is found with labeled data inside the model it explains. We ask whether such tools can be carried to other models through a map between residual streams fit only on unlabeled prompts. We transfer a refusal direction, tested causally by addition and ablation, and two read-out tools, a correctness direction and a sentiment probe, across 110 pairs of models from five families and 1B to 72B parameters and between base and instruction-tuned models, with controls for specificity and five seeds. How much transfers depends on what the map was fit on. A map fit on ordinary questions recovers 54\% of the target's own refusal steering and 16\% to 77\% of its correctness gain; adding unlabeled prompts from the region where the tool operates raises these to 102\% and 88\% to 98\%, while control directions recover at most 1\%. We prove that a linear map behaves this way whenever two models correspond linearly on the data it covers, and a label-free coverage score derived from this result tracks recovery across more than 16,000 runs and explains earlier reports that maps between models fail across domains. Carried read-out tools outperform anything the target's unlabeled representations yield. Interpretability results, once found, can be reused across models at the cost of a few unlabeled prompts.

title: EmoHarness: Boosting Multimodal Emotion Understanding with Meta-Harness Evolving
abstract: Small multimodal models can misjudge emotion when words, voice, and visual cues conflict. We present EmoHarness, which runs such a model, the frozen student, inside a harness: the prompts, settings, and verification code around its calls. A human-written starting harness, the scaffold, numbers the student's visual observations, transcript, and prosody descriptions as citable evidence and has the student weigh candidate emotions against it. In Meta-Harness Evolving (MHE), a stronger LLM, the Builder, reads the student's errors and execution traces offline and edits the harness; static checks and validation gates decide which edits are kept, and the Builder never sees evaluation items. On 5,507 MME-Emotion items, EmoHarness raises task-macro Recognition by 7.6-13.4 points over a single video-only call for all four students and both Builders. Transcripts and prosody descriptions supply most of this boost (+5.38 to +10.71); the scaffold changes the audio-augmented call by -0.79 to +2.54, partly through extra multi-label predictions, and evolved edits add at most +0.95, although no evolved increment survives Holm correction. The harness's emotion context also transfers to IntentQA, with small gains for three of four students, none of which survives correction. EmoHarness thus boosts small multimodal students chiefly by supplying and organizing audio-derived evidence.

title: AgentLSD: Evaluating AI Security Agents Under Adversarial Task Contamination
abstract: AI agents for security inspect web pages, source code, logs, configuration files, and command outputs. These environments may contain deceptive artifacts that influence the agent’s behavior. We call this adversarial task contamination. Whereas prompt injection relies on attacker-supplied instructions, task contamination also includes non-instructional evidence, such as fake results and decoy endpoints. We present AgentLSD, a controlled framework for studying adversarial task contamination. AgentLSD uses Capture the Flag (CTF) challenges as its experimental environment. We inject trap artifacts, such as fake flags, misleading hints, decoy endpoints, and hidden cues, while preserving the intended CTF solution. The framework supports paired clean and trap-augmented experiments with deterministic trap generation, runtime injection, telemetry, and delivery verification. We evaluate six models on 11 web CTF challenges. In the clean condition, agents capture 41% of the flags, and no model solves every challenge. We then measure the impact of task contamination. Even when the agent still recovers the flag, traps increase the number of turns (+20) and reasoning tokens (+2k). Solve-rate effects are more heterogeneous, as some model–challenge pairs are largely unaffected while others follow decoys or submit wrong flags. These results show that clean CTF performance understates vulnerability to deceptive task evidence. AgentLSD isolates this effect and provides a reproducible benchmark for studying it. We release the framework, configurations, trap specifications, and raw traces.

title: What Breaks Scribble-Supervised Segmentation? An Audit-Informed Benchmark for Scribble Annotation Robustness
abstract: Scribble-supervised segmentation is typically evaluated with a fixed annotation set, leaving robustness to distinct semantic and geometric imperfections poorly understood. Motivated by an audit of 12,031 manual PASCAL Visual Object Classes (VOC) 2012 scribbles and prior work, we introduce six controlled perturbation operators. Class corruption, spatial offset, and directional perturbation directly operationalize audit signals. Stroke-length reduction is motivated by prior scribble studies, while random dropout and fragmentation serve as diagnostic controls. Each operator reports requested and achieved changes. We evaluate manual and automatic scribbles across two image domains, two principal backbone settings, and multiple training pipelines, with an additional MiT-B1 PFA anchor evaluation. In the five-seed Tree Energy Loss (TEL)-ResNet101 VOC study, mean intersection over union (mIoU) drops from 70.08 to 1.46 under class corruption, compared with 35.57 for spatial offset, 52.20 for directional perturbation, and 63.24 for stroke-length reduction at their strongest settings. At the evaluated endpoints, semantic-anchor corruption produces the largest degradation, while geometric and support responses depend on the pipeline and dataset. Our benchmark provides a reproducible protocol for diagnosing annotation robustness beyond clean-set accuracy. The operator code is available at https://github.com/Wmhiram99/scribble-operator-benchmark.

title: LO-World: Unified BEV Latent Modeling for Joint 4D Occupancy and LiDAR Forecasting
abstract: LiDAR point clouds and 3D semantic occupancy represent two distinct modalities capturing fine-grained metric geometry and dense volumetric semantics, respectively, holding natural potential for mutual complementarity. However, existing world models typically forecast these modalities independently or cascade them heuristically, missing the opportunity for reciprocal cross-modal regularization. To address this, we propose LO-World, a unified 4D world model that forecasts both modalities within a shared BEV latent space. This single-stream formulation enables dense semantics and metric geometry to mutually reinforce each other, while eliminating multi-pipeline redundancy. Specifically, LO-World couples an efficient hybrid range-voxel autoencoder with a flow-matching generator that caches historical context to reduce iterative sampling latency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LO-World outperforms prior state-of-the-art baselines, improving occupancy forecasting IoU by 10.9% and reducing LiDAR Chamfer Distance by 30.1%. Meanwhile, it sustains a real-time throughput exceeding 25~FPS on a single RTX 4090. Our code is available at https://github.com/lzzzzzm/LO-World.

title: Controlled Binary Assignment Flows
abstract: This paper introduces a geometric approach to the representation and learning of time-variant parametrizations of deep assignment flows, for binary data labelings on graphs. Each edge carries an optimally controlled parameter flow in a 2-dimensional totally geodesic submanifold, based on objectives derived from a non-local linear scale space representation of the input data. The aggregation of triplets of such flows in 5-dimensional totally geodesic submanifolds is learned from data. The fusion of these flows determines the trajectory in the high-dimensional symmetric parameter space and by geometric integration the layers of binary deep assignment flows. Numerical results demonstrate the expressivity and the limitation of our highly parallel geometric local synthesis approach to high-dimensional deep assignment flow parametrizations.

title: Spectral Unlearning: Transformer Structure-Preserving Updates for Language Models
abstract: Machine unlearning in large language models (LLMs) aims to remove specific learned knowledge, capabilities, or behaviors while preserving model utility. Existing methods have mostly focused on the design of unlearning objectives, while largely overlooking the intrinsic matrix structure of transformer weights. In particular, standard optimizers operate on independent scalar coordinates, thereby ignoring this matrix structure. We propose spectral unlearning, an update framework that combines standard unlearning objectives with matrix-structured optimization. We show that the spectral update corresponds to the steepest-descent direction for transformers composed of linear layers with normalized inputs and outputs. Our approach is applied on top of existing unlearning methods and evaluated across complementary axes of memorization, privacy, and utility, summarized via their harmonic mean. Spectral unlearning consistently outperforms a broad range of baselines and closes most of the gap to a retain-trained reference. Code is available at https://github.com/unlearn-ml/spectral-unlearning/.

title: RML 1.2: Aligning RML with RDF 1.2 Triple Terms and Reifying Triples
abstract: RDF 1.2 introduces triple terms and the rdf:reifies property as a native mechanism for statement-level metadata. However, declarative mapping languages such as RML, which generate RDF from heterogeneous data sources, have not yet been aligned with this update: prior RDF-star extensions predate RDF 1.2's abstract data model and, furthermore, do not support its new directional language-tagged strings. This paper introduces RML 1.2, a backward-compatible extension of RML-Core for generating triple terms and directional language-tagged strings. We accompany the extension of RML with an open-source Python implementation and a suite of test cases.

title: Trade Promotion Optimisation for Consumer Goods
abstract: Trade promotions consume a large share of consumer-goods revenue, yet most planners still set discounts with a single, often unreliable, price elasticity per item. We present an end-to-end Trade Promotion Optimisation (TPO) system built as one chain: analogue SKUs, point elasticity, elasticity curve, price recommendation, promotional lift and net lift. Elasticity is measured at post-promo time from directional price-dip events against a rolling regular price, and at promo time by a causal estimator that residualises trend, seasonality and promotion, handles stock-out censoring with a Tobit likelihood and updates itself from the first clean promotion week. Items with weak evidence borrow the point elasticity and the curvature from analogue SKUs chosen by a cross-validated ridge model over category, brand, sub-category, price line and description. The optimiser separates self-price lift from substitution and post-promo dips and adjusts for inventory and trade funding. In a four-week promotion experiment on a 39-SKU consumer brand (mean elasticity -3.06), the plan lifts units by 20.6% and revenue by 6.9% at flat margin. Analogue pooling halves elasticity error relative to hierarchy averaging.

title: Training Vision Transformers to Focus: Emergence of Spatial Attention Head Specialization
abstract: Self-supervised learning in Vision Transformer models, such as DINO, enables robust visual perception without requiring labeled data by leveraging large-scale image datasets. However, these models lack a focusing mechanism during training, resulting in perceptual representations that are often ambiguous or overly similar. In this work, we introduce two visual focusing loss functions designed to establish correspondence between the model's attention and specific regions within images. Specifically, we leverage the multi-head attention mechanism within the model to selectively steer the model's focus, leading to the emergence of spatial attention head specialization, characterized by diverse and spatially focused perceptual capabilities without requiring annotations. Through both qualitative and quantitative evaluations, we demonstrate that our method substantially increases the spatial selectivity and diversity of attention heads, improving both interpretability and performance on dense prediction tasks such as zero-shot image segmentation.

title: Back-reference Analogy within Artificial Neural Networks Implementation
abstract: We are to address our past approach to tackling back-reference problem which is known to be NP-hard and, thus, impractical in general, however, the applicable and practical approach is required in order to make the search possible within the defined time frame, on that account we present our ‘in-deep’ concept which can be applied in the implementation of artificial neural networks (ANNs), this approach gives us the delay function which can be successfully used in the hypothetical networks, where the immediate transition between neural nodes is to be made delayed according to the structure and maybe even nature, we will further discuss how it can be vital for the newly presented ANNs

title: Certify, Report, or Refuse: Harm-Constrained Conformal Prediction for Clinical Actions
abstract: Routing a melanoma case to routine follow-up is a serious action error that diagnostic coverage alone does not rule out. We present Harm-Constrained Risk-Optimal Conformal Prediction (HC-ROCP), a training-free framework that uses frozen classifier probabilities and adds a harm penalty when choosing prediction sets and actions. We test the resulting policies on disjoint calibration splits with multiplicity adjustment. HC-ROCP certifies supported claims, reports descriptive fallback policies, and refuses unsupported subgroup claims. We evaluate these outputs retrospectively on COVID-19 radiographs, ISIC 2019 dermoscopy, and EyePACS-to-APTOS retinopathy transfer. Across ten calibration seeds, HC-ROCP reduces COVID-19 severe-action errors from the exact risk-optimal baseline's 4.68\% to 0.54\%. At a 5\% budget, global claims are certified for COVID-19 and ISIC, but the rare squamous-cell-carcinoma claim is refused. At 1\%, all settings receive descriptive reports. For each budget, we also report the minimum severe-case count needed to pass the global harm gate with zero errors, providing a starting point for further data collection.

title: Creative Priming: Decoupling Process from Product to Escape the Creative Paradox
abstract: Many of the most consequential advances promised by AI, from curing diseases and inventing new technologies to formulating new scientific theories, are fundamentally creative acts. Yet creativity is uniquely difficult to learn because it faces a creative paradox: learning to repeat past examples of creative success makes those specific examples more likely to recur, inhibiting the very creativity desired. This work argues that creativity is better modeled as an explicit process rather than as a property of individual artifacts, and proposes to learn the underlying generative principles behind the creative process. In particular, to escape the paradox, we introduce creative priming (CP), wherein a trained priming model generates a prompt-specific primer that assists a response model in being creative, explicitly decoupling the creative process from response generation. The priming model learns through GRPO, rewarding primers that lead to responses that are novel, high-quality, and diverse, thereby reinforcing the process that yields creative responses without reinforcing any specific response.

title: Benchmarking Constraint-Preserving QAOA for Renewable-Energy Portfolio Selection
abstract: We study renewable-energy portfolio selection using quantum approximate optimization algorithms (QAOA) with penalty-based X, cardinality-preserving XY, and sector-preserving XY mixers, benchmarked against exact and mixed-integer classical solvers. On 18 small primary problems, the mixers recovered optimal portfolios in 6, 13, and 15 cases, respectively; classical methods solved all 18 faster. The penalty-X baseline sampled almost uniformly among feasible portfolios, and a 72-run penalty sweep offered no reliable improvement. A second exploratory study used eight listed issuers across three dated problems; corrected 64-shot readouts recovered optima in 5 of 18 X settings and 16 of 18 XY settings. Financial backtests remained retrospective. Between May and October 2026, the baseline strategy returned −3.41%, while renewable/SPY blends returned +2.50% and +5.46%, below SPY’s +8.41%. Improved quantum sampling did not establish a speed advantage, independent validation, or investment alpha.

title: When Does Sliced Inference Pay Off? Resolution, Tiling and Dense Fusion for Small Object Detection
abstract: Sliced inference such as SAHI is the standard remedy for small objects in high-resolution imagery, but its gains are usually measured against low-resolution baselines. We revisit sliced inference with scale as the explicit variable and ask when tiling actually pays off. We compare seven dense detectors from four families on VisDrone and DOTA, under pre-specified hypotheses, calibration-only tuning and a single evaluation on held-out test data. Two findings emerge. First, much of the benefit attributed to slicing is a resolution effect: on VisDrone, a single pass trained at a higher resolution outperforms tiling with box fusion (merging decoded boxes) for every detector that could be trained at that resolution, and at equal compute a higher resolution helps more than a larger model. Second, tiles carry complementary information that box fusion wastes. We introduce SCAHI (Slicing with Coverage-Aware Hyper Inference), which accumulates the dense outputs of all passes with weights that give every image position the same total coverage, and reads objects off a peak grid fine enough to keep crowded neighbours apart. On identical passes, SCAHI outperforms box fusion for every YOLO detector on both datasets and matches it for FCOS. On DOTA, whose images far exceed the resolution a single pass can be trained at, tiles with SCAHI beat the best single pass for every detector, by 4.3 to 5.6 mAP50 at 2048 px, and replacing only SAHI's merge step by SCAHI adds 2.3 to 4.0 mAP50. An ablation attributes the gain to the border weighting and the resolution of the peak grid. Source code is available at https://github.com/beckerio/scahi.

We introduce SCAHI (Slicing with Coverage-Aware Hyper Inference), which accumulates the dense outputs of all passes with weights that give every image position the same total coverage, and reads objects off a peak grid fine enough to keep crowded neighbours apart. On identical passes, SCAHI outperforms box fusion for every YOLO detector on both datasets and matches it for FCOS. On DOTA, whose images far exceed the resolution a single pass can be trained at, tiles with SCAHI beat the best single pass for every detector, by 4.3 to 5.6 mAP50 at 2048 px, and replacing only SAHI's merge step by SCAHI adds 2.3 to 4.0 mAP50. An ablation attributes the gain to the border weighting and the resolution of the peak grid. Source code is available at https://github.com/beckerio/scahi.

title: Why LLMs Refuse to Summarize More in Long Contexts?
abstract: Abstract Long-horizon agents routinely exceed their context windows. A common form of context compaction that reduces a long interaction history to a smaller representation is to summarize the history and continue from the summary. This summarization loses information, and this loss is a common source of agent failures: forgotten details are rediscovered at extra cost or silently dropped. The natural repair is to ask for a longer summary, so we investigate whether that option actually works. Does summary length grow with input length? Across eleven models spanning coder, general-purpose, and reasoning families, summary length grows far more slowly than the input, so at 100k tokens, less than one percent of the input survives on both long documents and real agent trajectories. Furthermore, prompt-level directives do not close this gap: explicit length directives raise output only modestly, and the summary length plateaus far below the requested amount, however the request is phrased. To test whether training data can move this ceiling, we lightly fine-tune two models on summaries that differ only in length. The resulting output length shifts dramatically in either direction, tracking the finetuning summary length, even under a prompt that never mentions length. Consequently, this paper shows that summary length grows strongly sublinearly with input size, is only weakly responsive to length directives in the prompt, and is strongly responsive to fine-tuning, suggesting that training data, rather than the prompt, is the effective lever.

title: Simulation-aided Reinforcement Learning with Control Variates
abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms often rely on data collected from a target environment, which can be expensive and noisy. Although simulators can generate large amounts of additional data, standard simulation mixing approaches, which directly combine simulated and real experience, can degrade performance due to simulator inaccuracies, especially when they bias the solution away from the optimal policy. We propose a conservative simulation-aided learning method based on control variates, where simulated data is used solely to reduce variance in the learning process rather than directly shaping the learning target. We develop our approach for Policy-Evaluation, which is a fundamental building block of RL algorithms. Then we combine it within the actor-critic framework towards policy improvement, as well as extend it towards offline RL scenarios. Experiments on multiple MuJoCo benchmark tasks demonstrate improvements over standard simulation mixing approaches, highlighting control variates as an effective tool for simulation-aided reinforcement learning.

title: TrialDesignBench: Benchmarking Language Models for Phase-I Trial Design Against Clinical Knowledge
abstract: AI is used in much of the clinical trial pipeline. However, selecting the statistical design of a trial, a crucial step that determines how drug doses are tested on humans and evaluated, has seen almost no AI progress. LLMs appear to be a natural fit given their strengths in biomedical knowledge and statistical reasoning. Nevertheless, there is currently no appropriate way to evaluate such abilities because recent regulatory and methodological shifts, most notably FDA's Project Optimus, have redefined what constitutes a reasonable design and rendered many previous designs obsolete. To lay the groundwork for AI-assisted trial design, we introduce TrialDesignBench, a benchmark of 617 Phase-I/I-II oncology dose-finding trials, each paired with an expert-validated reference design that is consistent with the latest FDA regulatory initiatives. This reference standard is produced through a formalization of the expert design process. We evaluate five frontier LLMs, none of which matches the reference standard. Our ablation experiments trace this performance gap to two main causes, inference of latent, unrecorded design determinants from trial sources (supplying them raises class-wise balanced accuracy by 0.22) and structured decision-tree reasoning (+0.24). TrialDesignBench offers a reproducible, contemporary-standard objective for evaluating and enhancing AI-assisted trial design.

title: Learning to remember: advances in memory mechanisms for large language models
abstract: Abstract Memory has become a central mechanism for extending large language models (LLMs) beyond fixed context windows, stateless interaction, and static parametric knowledge. This survey organizes the literature around three complementary dimensions: the life cycle of memory, the storage substrate, and the system role that memory plays in LLM-based agents, while using cognitive-science-inspired memory concepts as a lightweight conceptual motivation rather than as a separate technical contribution or implementation family. On this basis, we distinguish three mechanism families: nonparametric memory, where information is stored outside model parameters in text, graph, multimodal, or database-like structures; parametric memory, where information is stored or accessed through activations, key-value caches, learned modules, adapter-based parameterizations, or model weights; and memory for agent evolution, where stored experiences support reinforcement learning, continual learning, procedural reuse, context engineering, and agent harness design. Evaluation is treated as a separate cross-cutting component rather than as a memory mechanism. Unlike surveys that focus primarily on retrieval-augmented generation or long-context modeling, this paper emphasizes the full memory life cycle: construction, maintenance, retrieval, consolidation, forgetting, governance, and evaluation. By aligning conceptual motivations, computational memory mechanisms, benchmarks, and deployment concerns, the survey provides a structured roadmap for designing memory-augmented LLM agents that are persistent, adaptive, auditable, and safe to update over time.

title: Emergence-Driven Security of LLM Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are no longer limited to text generators, but they can also plan, call tools, delegate tasks to other agents, act within external environments, and change states in response to their actions. In Anthropic’s recent report on an AI-orchestrated cyber-espionage campaign involving Claude Code, individual subtasks appeared legitimate when evaluated in isolation but became malicious when combined into an autonomous attack sequence. Consequently, the security of such complex LLM-based agentic systems may fail even when each component appears secure in isolation. This position and open-problem paper argues that LLM agent security should be studied as emergence-driven security: the analysis of security properties that arise from the interactions among agents and its components over time. We define emergence-driven security and provide a conceptual taxonomy to classify emergent security-related phenomena in LLM agents, covering both beneficial and harmful forms of emergence. Based on these insights, we propose EASE, an Emergence-Aware Security Evaluation framework that provides a systematic process for assessing how interactions among agents combine over time to produce harmful or beneficial system-level security outcomes. Finally, we conclude by outlining open problems for studying emergent behavior in LLM agents in the context of security. The paper is intended to provide a foundation for examining how the emerging capabilities and operational needs of LLM agents may shape security evaluations that go beyond static, model-level testing.

title: Beyond Sunny Skies: Using Large Language Models to Predict Urban Traffic in Adverse Weather
abstract: Urban traffic flow prediction is a cornerstone of intelligent transportation systems, yet accurate forecasting under adverse weather conditions remains a significant challenge. Existing data-driven models, while effective for routine patterns, often struggle with the sparse data and complex non-linear shifts associated with rare meteorological events. These methods typically treat environmental contexts as shallow numerical features, failing to capture the underlying semantic reasoning-why and how specific adverse conditions alter mobility behaviors across regions with different functional compositions. To address this limitation, we propose Multi-STG, a unified framework that integrates Large Language Model (LLM)-derived semantic priors with graph-based spatiotemporal learning. Multi-STG introduces an LLM-empowered semantic enhancement module that transforms comprehensive context descriptions such as weather, POIs, and holidays into high-level semantic embeddings, effectively providing a knowledge-driven complement to data scarcity. Furthermore, we design a multimodal attentional fusion mechanism to dynamically weigh heterogeneous inputs and a semantic-enhanced prediction head with gated residual calibration to robustly adjust forecasts based on semantic guidance. Extensive experiments on real-world multi-city private car datasets demonstrate that Multi-STG outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, reducing MAE by 11.82\% on average relative to the strongest baseline across three cities, while maintaining stable performance under sparse and non-stationary conditions.

title: How Far Does Second-Order Linear Response Predict Quantization Mismatch? Pre-Registered Measurements on Five Language Models
abstract: Serving systems choose a weight format for each model and deployment. A low-cost screen predicts the resulting KL divergence from the unquantized model's Fisher information using $\tfrac12Δ^\top FΔ$, the expansion underlying Hessian-aware and second-order post-training quantizers. We assess the reliability of this screen in GPU batches with channel-wise int8, per-tensor fp8 and group-wise int4 on Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-4B, OLMo-2-7B, Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-30B-A3B. Relative predictions hold across a 16-fold range of perturbation scales, int4 group sizes and rounding modes, while absolute predictions are heavy-tailed. A trimmed average brings 10 of 12 cells on Qwen3-4B and OLMo-2 within 15% of measured KL. The MoE model exhibits nonquadratic response at small perturbations, with int8 KL scaling as $α^{0.63}$. Computing per-sequence gradients in bf16 can cause fourfold prediction errors. We trace these errors to arithmetic in the lower half of the backward pass and eliminate them by using fp32 there. Batch-invariant kernels run at 0.55 times the throughput, while changes in reduction order introduce a floor of 0.17-0.22 nats per sequence. We build a screener with one streamed fp32 Fisher pass, trimmed tensor-block predictions with a band, a flag for aligned tensors and per-layer format allocation. On the unseen Mistral-7B-v0.3 family, all six predictions fall within the band, all three KL budgets are met, and vLLM throughput is predicted within 0.4%.

title: Adapting Small Language Models to Romanized Nepali: Tokenizer Fertility, Reference Likelihood, and Generation Metrics
abstract: Romanized Nepali, Nepali written in Latin script, is common in digital communication but has no standard spelling and few resources, and it is unclear how reliably small open language models can be adapted to it. We adapt three 2-3B base models from different families, Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-3B, and Gemma-2-2B, with QLoRA on 9,000 instruction examples produced by deterministic transliteration of Nepali instruction data. Each model is trained with one shared recipe and three seeds and evaluated on 1,000 held-out examples with reference-overlap metrics, byte-normalized reference likelihood (bits per byte, BPB), and an output audit, against zero-shot baselines under two prompts. Fine-tuning raises chrF++ from 10-14 to 29.0-30.6 and lowers BPB from 2.23-2.41 to 0.78-0.84; most zero-shot outputs (54-92%) are English-like. Likelihood and overlap disagree on how far apart the models are. Llama-3.2-3B has the lowest BPB in every seed, 0.042 below Qwen2.5-3B (95% CI 0.039-0.046), yet the two cannot be separated on chrF++ (30.51 and 30.61) or BLEU, even with paired item-level tests. Gemma-2-2B, whose tokenizer splits Romanized Nepali words least (2.72 tokens per word), scores worst on every measure. Which model gains most over its zero-shot baseline depends on the zero-shot prompt. In a supplementary comparison with an identical tokenizer, Llama-3.1-8B lowers BPB by 0.053 (0.050-0.056) relative to Llama-3.2-3B, while chrF++ and BLEU rise by only 0.68 and 0.58 points. Lower fertility and higher reference likelihood therefore did not identify the model whose outputs were closest to the references.

title: InferD: A Honeypot Framework for AI Inference Infrastructure
abstract: Large language model serving stacks, commercial inference APIs, vector databases, and agent orchestration gateways are now exposed on the public internet and indexed by commodity scanners within hours of deployment. The threat characteristics of this surface are only beginning to be measured, and the honeypot frameworks that could measure it were designed for conventional network services rather than for AI infrastructure. In fact, emulating an AI service is a distinct deception problem: the observable behavior of the service, including model inventories, token formats, tool-call protocols, and authorization flows, must be reproduced faithfully, while the underlying computation, model inference and tool execution, must never occur. We present InferD, a low-interaction honeypot framework organized around a single principle we call deception without inference: every request an adversary can observe is answered from static response pools, and nothing an adversary submits is ever executed. InferD decomposes the emulation into four deception planes, transport, service protocol, vulnerability surface, and agentic session, adds a provenance plane that links a planted credential to evidence of downstream model-mediated processing.

title: Spike-to-Field Mechanisms of Turbulence-Like Dynamics in Spatial Spiking Neural Networks
abstract: Neural avalanches and turbulence-like brain dynamics are usually measured after neural activity has been coarse-grained into continuous fields, leaving open which spike-level mechanisms can generate these macroscopic observables. We build a spatial leaky integrate-and-fire spiking neural network and explicitly transform spikes into activity-density and Hilbert phase fields. A delayed, distance-dependent, passive-dendrite regime reproducibly generates turbulence-like field structure, including high-amplitude phase-defect tracks, structure-function scaling, and power-law-favored continuous-field avalanche tails. Controls show that firing rate, vortex count, and avalanche tail fits are individually insufficient: destroying delayed propagation, dendritic filtering, or spike timing suppresses key field signatures, while random-space nulls can retain many mathematical phase defects but show weaker spatial structure and synaptic-delay transfer. Biologically motivated gates further shape the regime: PV-like perisomatic inhibition clamps phase dynamics, SST-like dendritic inhibition and projection-specific inhibitory facilitation preserve long-lived tracks, and a rate-constrained projection-STP regime expresses a roughly 200-ms episode at 12.25 Hz (full-record mean) across 12 seeds. These results use SNNs as a mechanistic testbed for spike-derived brain turbulence observables and show why phase defects and avalanche-like statistics must be interpreted jointly with spatial scaling and spike-level propagation.

title: HideOut - User Protection Against Localization with Throughput Guarantees in Mobile Networks
abstract: Channel state information (CSI) in cellular networks is primarily used to maintain quality of service (QoS), yet it leaks privacy-sensitive information, in particular the user equipment’s (UE) location. CSI is reported in plaintext on a publicly available schedule; thus, capturing it on the air and using a well trained AI model to localize the UE is straightforward. This simplicity in the attack execution makes it a serious privacy vulnerability. Using conventional privacy enhancing techniques, such as additive perturbation from differential privacy, to protect location data can potentially degrade the downlink communication quality. We present HideOut , a client-side defense mechanism that preserves the user’s location from neural-based localization methods, while maintaining their downlink Spectral Efficiency (SE). Unlike generic adversarial attacks, HideOut treats downlink SE as a strict constraint in an optimization setting. Under maximum ratio transmission (MRT) beamforming, we show that a user-selected SE loss budget can be converted into an angular rate-feasible constraint on the reported channel vector. HideOut then performs gradient-based localization obfuscation while projecting each update onto this rate-feasible set. We evaluate HideOut against four CSI-based localization architectures under both white-box and black-box assumptions. Across models, HideOut increases localization ambiguity (error) from approximately 1–2 m to 72–85 m while keeping downlink SE loss within a \(1\%\) budget. These results show that CSI-based localization can be substantially degraded at negligible communication quality loss when adversarial perturbations are made aware of the wireless link.

title: Towards Reconstructing and Recognizing Objects behind Fragmented Occlusion using Video
abstract: Perceiving objects through fragmented occlusions, such as foliage, is a natural capability of the human visual system but remains a fundamental challenge for computer vision. This work addresses the problem of object reconstruction, or de-occlusion, in the presence of high-density, fragmented occlusions. We propose a reconstruction framework that operates on a sequence of grayscale images of a moving object, acquired by a single camera, either stationary or in motion. The algorithm estimates the object's relative positions across frames by jointly registering the images and optimizing the alignment parameters to maximize the contrast of their average, referred to as the integrated image. This integrated image serves as the reconstructed representation of the object. Experimental evaluations on both synthetic and real video sequences demonstrate the feasibility of accurate reconstruction under occlusion densities exceeding 90%. The proposed approach is competitive with synthetic aperture techniques, which are limited to static objects and require complex camera setup with careful calibration. Furthermore, we show that the integrated image enables reliable object classification under severe occlusion when used as input to standard, off-the-shelf classifiers.

The proposed approach is competitive with synthetic aperture techniques, which are limited to static objects and require complex camera setup with careful calibration. Furthermore, we show that the integrated image enables reliable object classification under severe occlusion when used as input to standard, off-the-shelf classifiers.

title: Type-logical grammars and formal languages
abstract: We show that type-logical grammars with the standard rules for product, associativity, extraction and infixation have an NP-complete fixed recognition problem, adapting a construction for first-order linear logic from Pshenitsyn (2025), who already showed that grammars in first-order linear logic are closed under intersection and therefore not semilinear and not mildly context-sensitive. We strengthen these results and shown that grammars in first-order linear logic can simulate the quasi-linear grammars of Book \& Greibach (1970), the grammars recognised in non-deterministic linear time (NSPACE(n) or. NLIN). I argue that NLIN is an interesting class of formal languages as well, and a useful upper bound on the time complexity of formalisms used for natural language, just like LOGCFL is a useful upper bound on the space complexity. Taken together this means that first-order linear logic can be seen as the logic of non-deterministic linear-time string languages, graph languages and automata.

title: Le GENSA (GENeric Sensory Automaton): un modèle mathématique des interactions dynamiques par affinité en biologie
abstract: This presentation revisits the paper 'The Generic Sensory Automaton (GENSA) for modeling affinity-based dynamics and interactions in biology', by Pastor et Thomas-Vaslin. In this talk, for further dissemination and exchanges, we present and discuss the GENSA (GENeric Sensory Automaton), a mathematical framework aimed at modeling biological systems, like the immune system. The GENSA is an automaton capable of detecting and responding to environmental changes and thus, capable of perceiving and responding to events in its surrounding. The capacity of the GENSA to detect events in its environment, and modify its state accordingly, is formalized through mathematical notions of specificity and sensitivity. We give and discuss two fundamental GENSAs: the Neyman-Pearson GENSA (NP-GENSA) and the Random Distortion Testing GENSA (RDT-GENSA). These two GENSAs embed distinct decision types and satisfy functional redundancy, in a sense close to the biological notion of degeneracy. We will present some prospects this model opens, especially with degeneracy. The possibility to construct networks of GENSAs and the perspectives these networks open will also be discussed, beyond the conclusions of the initial paper.

title: Graph-Guided Bayesian Factor Analysis: A Fast Integrated EFA-CFA Approach for High-Dimensional Data
abstract: Factor analysis has been central to the analysis of high-dimensional biomedical data. However, existing exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis methods face several limitations: less interpretable factor findings, difficulty in identifying which variables can and cannot be represented by low-dimensional factors, challenges in estimating the covariance among factors, and maximum-likelihood fits that break down when variables outnumber subjects. We propose graph-guided Bayesian factor analysis (gg-BFA) to address these gaps. We first use a Bayesian model to explore and learn the latent graph structure, identifying which variables can and cannot be represented by low-dimensional factors and how many factors are needed. A dense-subgraph search proposes partitions of the variables into communities, each defining one factor, and a forward stepwise search compares their fractional variational posteriors and stops when the evidence lower bound first decreases. We show that this search recovers the true communities even when the number of variables grows much faster than the sample size. We then develop a confirmatory Bayesian model whose variational posterior of the covariance contracts at the parametric rate up to a logarithmic factor, yielding posterior inference for the factors and their covariance, as well as predictions of missing values. Its four members range from a community mask to several cross-loadings per variable. In five biomedical panels, the complete analysis took under ten minutes each on one GPU, and cross-loadings improved held-out covariance and the prediction of masked measurements. In TCGA Kidney, six of the first eight factors were enriched for known pathways, and 190 of the 210 factor correlations had 95% credible intervals excluding zero. Overall, gg-BFA is computationally fast and provides interpretable factor analysis findings and reliable inference results.

title: Foundation Training vs Localised Adaptation for Australian Sovereign AI
abstract: Foundation Training vs Localised Adaptation for Australian Sovereign AI Document Type: Technical Brief / Policy Note Subject: Sovereign Artificial Intelligence, Large Language Models (LLMs), Data Adaptation Geographic Scope: Australia Technical Summary Building frontier-grade foundation models (such as Mistral or Meta's open weights) from scratch requires multi-million dollar compute budgets and extensive web-scale datasets. For an Australian sovereign AI strategy, a viable and resource-efficient path relies on localised adaptation rather than full foundation training: Base Infrastructure: Leveraging established open-weight architectures (e.g., Meta's Muse Spark Open or similar open-weights foundation models) as the structural foundation. Domain & Cultural Fine-Tuning: Continuously fine-tuning these base models on high-quality, domain-specific Australian datasets, including: Legal & Regulatory Corpora: AustLII (Australasian Legal Information Institute) databases, Commonwealth and state legislation, ASIC, and APRA policy frameworks. Regional Nuance: Local vernacular, regional dialects, and Australian cultural context. Web Infrastructure Data: Systematic crawls of .au web domains to reflect domestic institutions and societal discourse. Model Agnosticism & Upgradability: A key advantage of localised adaptation (e.g., parameter-efficient fine-tuning like LoRA) is modularity. The domain-specific fine-tuning weights, custom datasets, and alignment layers can be preserved and adapted seamlessly whenever underlying open-weight base models are updated, upgraded, or replaced. By decoupling the high capital expenditure of pre-training base models from the localised alignment phase, Australia can achieve functional AI sovereignty, data governance, and domain accuracy on local compute infrastructure without duplicating foundational compute costs.

title: Double Blind Evals: Resolving the Dual Confidentiality Dilemma in AI Safety Auditing
abstract: AI safety evaluations often involve sensitive prompts and proprietary models. Evaluators want to keep their evaluation prompts secret from model owners to prevent purposeful or incidental data leakage, ensuring longer usefulness of their benchmark. Model owners in turn wish to keep their proprietary model weights and inference code within their own secure infrastructure to protect their IP. We present a way forward for "double-blind evals", which provide cryptographic guarantees that an evaluator's prompts are not shared with the model owner, while simultaneously maintaining the confidentiality of the model weights and inference code. To accomplish this, we use secure enclaves that encrypt data in RAM at the hardware level. In a world-first pilot, we test this approach by evaluating a proprietary Google DeepMind model (Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite) against a selection of the private AILuminate benchmark corpus, using an NVIDIA H100 secure enclave on Google Cloud Platform, and using OpenMined's PySyft to maintain data and model privacy. We believe this effort marks the first use of this technology to provide mutual secrecy for one organization's frontier-class proprietary model weights and another organization's closed benchmark.

title: Comparative Timing Characterization of Early-Exit and Fixed-Work Secret Comparisons on ESP32 and ESP8266
abstract: Abstract An early-exit secret comparison can expose matching-prefix length through execution timing. We quantify this behavior for 16-byte early-exit comparisons and a fixed-work XOR/OR alternative on ESP32 and ESP8266 microcontrollers. Internal CPU-cycle measurements were collected for prefix lengths 0–16 under two interrupt/barrier configurations, yielding 40,800 observations. Across prefix lengths 0–15, early-exit median timing rose by 40 cycles per matching byte on ESP32 and 25 on ESP8266. In the recorded sessions, 63 of 68 early-exit groups contained 300 identical readings, and all 17 group medians were distinct within each configuration. Fixed-work median timing did not vary with prefix length, although occasional elevated observations remained. These measurements characterize implementation-specific on-device timing leakage and the cost of the fixed-work routine; they neither establish binary-level constant-time behavior nor demonstrate a remotely observable attack.

title: Direct Conditioning of Audio Diffusion Transformers on fMRI Reveals Cortical Contributions to Sound Reconstruction
abstract: Reconstructing audio from brain activity remains challenging. Existing brain-to-audio pipelines typically map neural responses to predefined stimulus representations before synthesis. While recent work in the visual domain has explored direct conditioning on brain activity, this approach has not yet been extended to audio diffusion models. We introduce MAAS (Multi-Area Auditory Synthesis), an end-to-end framework that conditions a pretrained audio diffusion transformer on ROI-wise fMRI responses without first supervising a decoder to predict an external stimulus representation. MAAS uses region-specific projections and learned brain tokens to condition Stable Audio through a dedicated cross-attention pathway. On a 7T fMRI dataset, we demonstrate consistent improvements over baselines, including two-stage fMRI-to-latent conditioning, across both acoustic and semantic evaluation metrics. In addition, we introduce a fidelity metric grounded in a computational model of auditory neural processing, which allows us to quantify the contribution of individual auditory cortical regions to reconstructed audio representations.

title: attribution-calibration: error rates for directed attribution claims about multi-agent logs
abstract: A detector-agnostic harness that attaches an error rate to a directed attribution or influence claim about a multi-agent log. The user supplies their own detector and their own event log and gets back a family-wise error rate measured on surrogates built from that same log, a power curve from a spike-in positive control, and a detection floor reported with an explicit status. Every rate carries a Wilson interval. Four surrogates are provided, including the conventional circular-shift recipe, which is implemented faithfully in order to be measured against: it does not hold the actor sequence fixed, and on turn-ordered agent chat it was found to certify at least one influence edge on 90 per cent of structure-free replicates against a nominal 5 per cent.

title: Unmasking Four Knapsack Problems in the Traveling Thief Benchmark
abstract: The traveling thief problem (TTP) asks a thief to choose a tour and a packing together, and the benchmark of 9,720 instances of Polyakovskiy et al. (2014) is the standard test set for comparing TTP heuristics. We show that four of these instances are not TTP instances at all. Their files give a renting rate of 0.00, so the tour has no effect on the objective and each instance reduces to a 0-1 knapsack problem. One of them belongs to the 60 categorized instances on which new methods are usually compared, and on it five of nine published methods report exactly the same value. The cause is the format of the files, which keep the renting rate with two decimals, while the rule of the generator gives a rate close to 0.003 on these instances. The same rounding may shift the rate of 949 other instances by more than 1%. Since the tour and the packing used by the generator were not published, the original rates cannot be recovered. We therefore define new rates with the same rule, applied to a fully specified reference solution that we publish, and we show with a published heuristic that the corrected instances behave as TTP instances again. We also give reference results on the corrected instances and recommendations for future studies. Finally, we present ttplib, a new open-source Python library that loads any of the 9,720 instances, including the corrected ones, without downloading the whole benchmark.

title: Fairness in Explainable AI Narratives: Decomposing Social Disparities in LLM-Generated Explanations
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to translate technical explainable AI (XAI) artefacts such as SHAP into explanatory narratives (XAINs) for lay users. In high-risk domains, these explanations are often the main resource through which individuals can understand and contest adverse decisions. Yet LLMs are known to reproduce social bias, even from proxy variables alone, and fairness in XAINs remains unstudied. Because XAINs are bound to a ground-truth artefact, fairness concerns not only what a narrative says and how, but also whether it is equally faithful across social groups. We introduce fairness in XAINs as a new field of research and propose a framework that generates narratives under three conditions (protected attribute disclosed, withheld, or counterfactually swapped), allowing five comparisons that pinpoint the cause of disparities. We apply it to adversely classified instances from four datasets in credit scoring, education and employment, generating narratives with five LLMs, and evaluate faithfulness, feature coverage and sentiment. We find significant disparities across all datasets, metric families and models, arising in two ways. Faithfulness disparities result from feature values: LLMs make plausible but false statements, triggered by values that are unequally distributed across social groups. Feature coverage and sentiment disparities stem from the protected attribute itself: once it is disclosed, LLMs give less explanation to, or frame more negatively the narratives of, groups that have historically been discriminated against or are stereotypically associated with worse outcomes. A more faithful model removes the faithfulness disparities, and withholding protected attributes mostly removes the others, but neither suffices on its own. Fairness in XAINs should therefore be audited separately from the predictive model and its XAI artefact.

title: An EEG Emotion Recognition and Classification Method Based on MSRA and Bidirectional LSTM
abstract: EEG-based emotion recognition faces challenges from signal non-stationarity, low signal-to-noise ratios, inter-subject variability, and ambiguous emotional boundaries. To address these issues, this study proposes an approach that combines the Multi-Taper Method (MTM) and Welch method for power spectral density (PSD) feature extraction and combines the Multi-Scale Residual Attention and Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (MSRA-BiLSTM) for emotion recognition. The approach captures spatial and frequency-band features while learning temporal dependencies. Experiments on three-class classification using the DEAP dataset achieved accuracies of 98.03%, 97.54%, and 96.81% for Valence, Arousal, and Dominance, respectively, with Macro-F1 scores of 0.9789, 0.9749, and 0.9674. The overall accuracy was 97.46%, outperforming conventional Welch-based features, differential entropy features, and end-to-end training. Therefore, the study has contributed to the problem of emotion recognition based on EEG signals.

title: TRACE: Adaptive Trust-Region Bayesian Optimization for Open-Ended Molecular Design
abstract: Optimizing molecules under small evaluation budgets requires deciding both where in chemical space to search and which candidate within that region to evaluate. We introduce Trust Region Adaptive Chemical Exploration (TRACE), a framework for open-ended molecular Bayesian optimization (BO), where candidates are generated on demand rather than selected from a fixed library. TRACE combines an objective-free graph-perturbation mechanism with a fixed, chemistry-aware Gaussian process (GP) surrogate using fragprints, a representation combining molecular fingerprints and fragment descriptors. Rather than learning the search geometry itself, TRACE makes the scale of chemical exploration explicit through a Tanimoto-similarity threshold controlling chemical extent and a cardinality budget controlling candidate-search breadth. A simple success/failure controller expands or contracts both quantities during optimization, while the GP and acquisition function select which admissible molecules to evaluate. Across six challenging molecular optimization benchmarks under matched 1,000-evaluation budgets, TRACE achieves the strongest overall sample efficiency as measured by the best molecule found as evaluations accumulate. Crossed ablations on two objectives further show that adaptive region control contributes beyond the proposal mechanism, while its benefit depends on the proposal distribution. We further apply TRACE to the stability of iron phthalocyanine (FePc), a non-precious molecular electrocatalyst whose degradation can involve loss of the Fe center. Using a first-principles density functional theory (DFT) workflow designed for accurate energy evaluation, TRACE increases the computed thermodynamic resistance to Fe dissolution from 0.42 to 2.59 eV over 80 designed evaluations.

title: Individualized antibiotic discontinuation support using machine learning: hospital- wide evaluation of gradient boosting and LSTM models
abstract: Abstract Background Prolonged antibiotic therapy contributes to antimicrobial resistance and may increase the risk of adverse effects in hospitalized patients. Timely antibiotic discontinuation is an important quality and safety goal; however, identifying the optimal time to stop treatment remains challenging. Machine learning models trained on routinely collected clinical data may provide data-driven decision support to identify patients in whom antibiotic discontinuation could be considered. This study developed and evaluated two machine learning approaches to predict antibiotic discontinuation in hospitalised, non-critically ill patients. Methods A retrospective cohort study was conducted using daily laboratory results and vital signs from hospitalized patients receiving antibiotic therapy at a large academic centre. Two models were developed: an XGBoost model operating on daily patient snapshots enriched with temporal features; and a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network processing raw daily clinical sequence. Model performance was evaluated primarily using the Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC), alongside other metrics. Predictions were evaluated using a two-day anticipation window, with predictions considered to be correct when generated on the day of clinician-initiated antibiotic discontinuation or up to two days earlier. Model interpretability was assessed using SHAP (XGBoost) and Integrated Gradients (LSTM). Results The XGBoost model achieved an AUPRC of 0.579, while the LSTM achieved an AUPRC of 0.480 (prevalence-based baseline 0.385) Sensitivity was 41.2% for XGBoost and 19.6% for the LSTM, while precision was 58.5% and 55.5%, respectively. Feature importance analyses showed that infection-related features, such as C-reactive protein and temperature, were among the most influential predictors in both models. Oxygen saturation was also highly influential, alongside data-availability patterns and other clinical variables. Conclusions Both models demonstrated the feasibility of identifying clinical patterns preceding clinician-initiated antibiotic discontinuation from routinely collected clinical data. The two models showed different performances across the evaluated metrics, with XGBoost achieving better performance than the LSTM. By identifying a subset of patients up to two days before clinician-initiated discontinuation, these models could support earlier clinical reassessment of ongoing antibiotic therapy. The models were designed as clinician-in-the-loop decision-support tools rather than autonomous systems. Prospective validation is needed to determine whether model-guided reassessment can safely facilitate earlier antibiotic discontinuation.

evidence.abstract: Abstract Background Prolonged antibiotic therapy contributes to antimicrobial resistance and may increase the risk of adverse effects in hospitalized patients. Timely antibiotic discontinuation is an important quality and safety goal; however, identifying the optimal time to stop treatment remains challenging. Machine learning models trained on routinely collected clinical data may provide data-driven decision support to identify patients in whom antibiotic discontinuation could be considered. This study developed and evaluated two machine learning approaches to predict antibiotic discontinuation in hospitalised, non-critically ill patients. Methods A retrospective cohort study was conducted using daily laboratory results and vital signs from hospitalized patients receiving antibiotic therapy at a large academic centre. Two models were developed: an XGBoost model operating on daily patient snapshots enriched with temporal features; and a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network processing raw daily clinical sequence. Model performance was evaluated primarily using the Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC), alongside other metrics. Predictions were evaluated using a two-day anticipation window, with predictions considered to be correct when generated on the day of clinician-initiated antibiotic discontinuation or up to two days earlier. Model interpretability was assessed using SHAP (XGBoost) and Integrated Gradients (LSTM). Results The XGBoost model achieved an AUPRC of 0.579, while the LSTM achieved an AUPRC of 0.480 (prevalence-based baseline 0.385) Sensitivity was 41.2% for XGBoost and 19.6% for the LSTM, while precision was 58.5% and 55.5%, respectively. Feature importance analyses showed that infection-related features, such as C-reactive protein and temperature, were among the most influential predictors in both models. Oxygen saturation was also highly influential, alongside data-availability patterns and other clinical variables. Conclusions Both models demonstrated the feasibility of identifying clinical patterns preceding clinician-initiated antibiotic discontinuation from routinely collected clinical data. The two models showed different performances across the evaluated metrics, with XGBoost achieving better performance than the LSTM. By identifying a subset of patients up to two days before clinician-initiated discontinuation, these models could support earlier clinical reassessment of ongoing antibiotic therapy. The models were designed as clinician-in-the-loop decision-support tools rather than autonomous systems. Prospective validation is needed to determine whether model-guided reassessment can safely facilitate earlier antibiotic discontinuation.

title: AgentOPSD: Turn-Level Credit Assignment via Recursive Belief Revision
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards ordinarily spreads a single advantage over a whole trajectory, a granularity too coarse to isolate the few decisions on which success in a long, multi-turn interaction actually turns. Privileged self-distillation supplies denser supervision, but it leaves unanswered how a set of local teacher-student discrepancies should be converted into credit along a sequence. We introduce AgentOPSD, a critic-free scheme that assigns credit recursively, one interaction turn at a time. Inside a turn, the token-level log-probability gaps between a skill-conditioned self-teacher and the student are summed, and that sum acts as evidence in a recursive Bayesian update carried out in log-odds space; the resulting revisions reallocate the outcome-derived advantage across turns through a multiplier that is bounded and preserves its sign. With Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-7B as policy backbones on ALFWorld, the method improves consistently on GRPO and on self-distillation baselines, and attains 89.1% success at the 7B scale. Ablations attribute the gain to aggregating evidence at turn boundaries and to making the belief revision depend on history, rather than to the local gap by itself.

title: Whose Bytes Were Hashed? An Audit Checklist for AI Verifiability Claims, with a DEUSPROOF Case
abstract: Services that advertise "verifiable AI output" do not always say which bytes are actually covered. This note turns that question into a six-item checklist - external anchoring, content hashing and its published normalization rules, score reproducibility, identity custody, governance records, and data retention - and permits only three verdicts: reproducible, not reproducible, or inconsistent with the published figure. One case is examined: certificate 46c2ac75 (DEUSPROOF). Its ledger entry can be recomputed by anyone from the published preimage (SHA-256 = a29dc96f...), while the certificate output_hash cannot: the signed text was removed from the record on 20 October 2026 (a public field, content_removed_at), so the same published rule applied to the text the platform API returns today yields 54463ae5... rather than 9bfdd072.... Both halves are reported together. The sample covers a single service at a single point in time, and two checklist items rest only on the written statements of the operator.

title: From Likelihood Convergence to Parameter Convergence in POMDPs
abstract: Likelihood-based methods are widely used to learn the parameters of partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). While finite-sample guarantees for policy suboptimality exist for certain POMDP subclasses, analogous guarantees for parameter recovery remain less well understood. For any candidate POMDP parameter, we bound its parameter recovery error in terms of its likelihood gap to the ground truth, the structural conditioning of the observation and transition kernels, and the behavior policy used to collect data. The bound applies in both the undercomplete and overcomplete regimes, with the latter following naturally from the undercomplete analysis. Because the result applies to any sufficiently good candidate, it yields finite-sample guarantees for the maximum-likelihood estimator and any procedure producing a parameter with controlled likelihood gap. This is particularly useful for near-optimal learning in infinite-horizon POMDPs, where existing approaches largely rely on model-based planning with accurate transition and observation kernel estimates. The bound separates the contributions of the behavior policy and model, showing how data-collection choices, including action coverage, and their effects on mixing can accelerate parameter learning.

title: AI Framework for Fair and Auditable Prior Authorization
abstract: Prior authorization is a critical function in health insurance; however, traditional processes regularly cause operational delays, member dissatisfaction, inconsistent denials, provider frustration, delayed access to care, and increased regulatory scrutiny. Current authorization workflows are often overloaded by manual reviews, unclear policies, fragmented clinical documentation, limited decision transparency, and insufficient visibility into denial reasons. As health insurers adopt AI-enabled automation, these challenges become more complex if decisions are not explainable, evidence-based, auditable, and supported by human oversight. This study introduces a secure AI-driven decision-support framework for prior authorization that integrates explainable decision logic, policy-rule traceability, clinical-evidence mapping, bias monitoring, human review checkpoints, and appeal-ready explanations within a single governance model. Unlike automation focused mainly on speed and cost, the proposed framework prioritizes fair, transparent, and accountable decision-making across the authorization lifecycle. Each AI recommendation explains why it was made and links the decision to medical guidelines, policy rules, supporting evidence, prior reviewer actions, and member-specific details. The framework is expected to reduce authorization turnaround time, decrease avoidable denials, reduce appeal overturns, improve provider and member satisfaction, and make decisions more consistent and fairer across clinical and demographic groups.
