title: Understanding Spike Encoding across IoT Sensing Modalities: An Empirical Study
abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer a path to energy-efficient sensing on Internet of Things (IoT) devices. The input encoder shapes that opportunity by changing the cues available for recognition and the work required to process them. We study these choices across wireless, inertial, surface electromyographic, and tactile sensing. For wireless activity recognition, interleaving reduces estimated energy for arithmetic in the network layers, latency from the prepared input window to returned scores, and energy on the graphics processing unit and system-on-chip (GPU/SoC) rail, compared with repeating the full window on Jetson AGX Orin. With the same input size at each SNN time step, repeating a compact input can yield higher mean development accuracy than interleaving. The inertial experiments show that higher accuracy can come at higher device cost. Direct input can also be faster and more accurate than an event encoder while using less energy on the measured rail, even when its estimated energy for arithmetic in the network layers is higher. Level crossings improve grasp recognition on a later day for previously observed users. In tactile slip detection, level crossings shift the balance between missed slips and false alarms, and checkpoint selection can reverse which input offers higher slip recall. We use these findings to outline how edge sensing systems can profile encoders against the signal structure, the errors that matter to the task, and the cost of the full inference pipeline.

title: Food Information and Competitive Performance of Evolved Behavioral Programs in a Spatial Digital-Evolution Model
abstract: Inherited program growth does not by itself establish adaptive function. We developed a spatial digital-evolution model and used neutral inheritance controls followed by frozen-program competition to distinguish sequence growth from the competitive contribution of food information. An initial functional study tested the predominant programs of 90 source populations in 540 competitions. Intact programs generally outperformed information-withheld versions that retained the same per-call scanning cost, and also outperformed the ancestor under the tested conditions. We then independently evolved 90 additional source populations and performed 1,800 further competitions on two fresh maps per source with complementary founder assignments. At baseline, intact-minus-withheld differences were 1.83, 1.99, 1.88 living descendants per founder across scattered, small-patch and large-patch resources. The baseline information-benefit result recurred in all three layouts. Across five assay settings per layout, including one-at-a-time changes in regeneration interval and scanning price, 15/15 pointwise bootstrap intervals were above zero. Sources evolved only under baseline conditions. The assays excluded predators and measured performance over 600 steps, so their results support a conditional functional benefit of usable food information rather than general fitness, increased complexity or ecosystem stability. Independent seeds and parameter sensitivity strengthen internal evidence, while the literature contribution and wider applicability remain bounded. AI use: Generative AI assisted with design, implementation, analysis, model verification, literature searches and writing. This is an author-review draft, not a peer-reviewed publication. The supplementary archive covers independent validation v0.7; earlier study data are retained separately.

title: ReGKG-2025: A GKG-Compatible Reconstruction of the GDELT Global Knowledge Graph for the Missing Period of 14 June to 2 July 2025
abstract: The June 2025 outage in the Global Database of Events, Language, and Tone (GDELT) collection pipeline left a gap in the Global Knowledge Graph (GKG), interrupting article-level news metadata used in downstream research. ReGKG-2025 is an archive-derived sample of 281,620 reconstructed article records covering all 1,665 missing 15-minute batches. Articles were recovered from Common Crawl and the Wayback Machine using source quotas estimated from surrounding native GKG data. Text was screened and normalized, non-English bodies were translated, and flagged records were manually reviewed. Eligible articles were converted to the 27-column GKG 2.1 layout. The versioned package includes record-level provenance, archive replay and WARC locators, source summaries, source-by-day calibration weights, and the complete manual decision journal. The sample reaches about 14% of modeled native volume and represents sources accounting for 84% of selected reference record mass. In an intact-week test, 41% of recovered articles matched native GKG records; field agreement on matched pairs is close to the processor baseline (tone MAE 1.69). The dataset supports retrospective content analysis and source-level aggregates; its tone and theme distributions differ from native GKG, and it does not support exhaustive counts. Data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23964265.

title: Shape-Adaptive Subspace-Constrained Quadratic Matrix Factorization
abstract: Quadratic manifold fitting provides a flexible framework for modeling nonlinear low-dimensional structures embedded in high-dimensional spaces. However, existing methods typically employ prescribed noise models or fixed loss functions, limiting their adaptability to varying noise characteristics. To address this limitation, we propose an alternating maximum likelihood estimation method for subspace-constrained quadratic matrix factorization, termed AMLE-SQMF, which jointly estimates the quadratic manifold and the underlying noise distribution. Specifically, we model the residuals using a generalized Gaussian distribution (GGD), whose shape parameter controls the tail behavior and determines the associated fitting loss. By exploiting the closed-form maximum likelihood estimator of the scale parameter, we eliminate the scale variable and derive a profile negative log-likelihood. Based on this formulation, we develop an alternating optimization algorithm that iteratively updates the manifold parameters and estimates the noise shape parameter. This enables adaptive loss selection within a unified likelihood-based framework, without requiring prior specification of the noise characteristics. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of AMLE-SQMF in quadratic manifold fitting and its robustness to diverse noise distributions.

title: Replicating Sparks of Weight-Space Programming with Claude: logs, networks, scores and harness
abstract: The complete logs, networks, scores and code of a replication of Experiments 1-7 of Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights (Takehi, Teoh, Zhang and Khattab, MIT CSAIL, 2026), run with Claude Opus 5.5 through the Claude Code CLI, using the original prompts word for word and the original effort levels. For every conversation: everything sent to the model, everything it returned (with reasoning summaries and the raw CLI event stream), every code run with its output, the networks it wrote, and the scoring. Also included: the harness (validated against the original logs by replaying the original model's answers), the rebuilt Go opponents of Experiment 6, and the validation results. title: ScrapeBench: Evaluating Legal Compliance of AI Agents in Website Scraping
abstract: AI agents deployed on the open web are becoming more capable of performing actions that may breach contractual provisions and violate computer security laws. In this paper, we introduce ScrapeBench, the first agentic benchmark for empirically evaluating the legal compliance of AI agents with website scraping policies, namely terms of service (ToS) and robots.txt directives. Across widely used closed-weight and open-weight AI agents, we find that most agents exhibit low compliance rates (< 5%) when instructed to scrape websites in our sample of 1,626 popular websites that explicitly prohibit scraping. In addition, we observe that even where AI agents actively check the applicable ToS and robots.txt, they continue to exhibit low compliance rates. Conversely, in our sample of 269 websites that do not prohibit scraping, we observe that agents sometimes refuse to scrape despite it being lawful, such as Claude Opus 4.6 exhibiting an over-refusal rate of 98.5%. Our human baseline experiments (n = 180 participants) suggest that humans exhibit compliance rates comparable to AI agents but over-refuse at much higher rates.

title: Least-Privilege Auditing of Agent Tool Calls with Intent Graphs and Reasoning-Guided Escalation
abstract: LLM agents that call tools are exposed to indirect prompt injection: instructions hidden in tool outputs can steer an agent into calls the user never asked for. We present a runtime audit that derives an executable intent graph from the user's objective and the deployment's tool catalog with one LLM call per task, and checks every tool call against it with a deterministic loop that makes no LLM call (median 5.7 microseconds per call). Two further mechanisms recover utility. Lookups of the user's own state bypass the audit, because the harm of an attack lies in its write or outward step. title: GRAIL-VN: A Graph-Grounded Runtime-Verifiable Agentic Framework for Reliable Branching Visual Novel Script Generation
abstract: The core challenge in visual novel script generation lies not only in generating coherent narrative content, but also in continuously maintaining the consistency of branching structures, character states, and conditional logic as the story evolves. This paper proposes GRAIL-VN, a Graph-Grounded Runtime-Verifiable Agentic Framework for Reliable Branching Visual Novel Script Generation, which models visual novel script generation as an iterative update process based on narrative state. The framework maintains persistent narrative state through a Narrative World Graph (NWG), performs state retrieval, local generation, and state commitment through a graph-backed iterative runtime (GIR), and applies multi-layer runtime verification before updates are written back through Plan-Graph-Constrain-Realize (PGCR); Lookahead Branch Planning (LBP) and Just-In-Time Casting (JITC) further support lookahead branch decision-making and dynamic expansion of the narrative world. We conduct experiments on 36 narrative briefs covering different genres and complexity levels, and perform an integrated analysis combining automated structural evaluation, LLM pairwise narrative quality evaluation, and goal achievement evaluation. The results show that the value of the persistent graph mainly comes from its continuous participation as a runtime state interface, rather than from one-time reading during the generation stage; PGCR can effectively detect and repair inconsistent updates, thereby improving generation reliability, while LBP and JITC further enhance branch planning and dynamic expansion capabilities. Overall, GRAIL-VN provides a unified runtime framework for reliable branching visual novel script generation.

title: TransArt3D: From Two States to Articulated 3D Reconstruction with Video Transition Priors
abstract: Reconstructing interactable articulated assets from a few images is key to robotics and simulation, yet highly underconstrained. Existing optimization-based methods fit an articulated asset under a static 3D prior that scores each state independently, so per-state reconstruction errors leak into the estimated moving part and joint as false motion. Video diffusion models capture how objects move between states, but only implicitly in 2D. To this end, we present TransArt3D, an optimization-based framework that reconstructs an articulated 3D asset from two endpoint images by translating this video transition prior into explicit part structure and joint kinematics. It first lifts frames generated between the endpoints with a transition-coupled 3D consensus that applies the static 3D prior jointly across frames, stabilizing unchanging regions and initializing the parts and joint. A rectified-flow kinematic refinement then lets the video prior supervise a 3D motion field over the whole transition, while part assignment and a shared joint constrain the field throughout optimization, keeping per-state errors out of the articulation. Finally, a motion-aware canonical appearance fusion uses the recovered articulation to map both endpoint images onto one canonical surface, texturing regions that only one state reveals. On PartNet-Mobility, TransArt3D outperforms methods given the same two endpoints in geometry and joint accuracy, and surpasses methods given six observed states in articulated-state geometry, joint localization and appearance.

title: Alignment of Agentic Systems
abstract: In this article, we present a novel bottom-up approach to aligning agentic systems. Additionally,we introduce a training algorithm called projective learning, inspired by how the brain likely learns.To start, we describe two seemingly universal neuronal models, capable of modeling a broad rangeof phenomena, with the aim of modeling consciousness in our systems.We then develop projective learning, a mechanism that utilizes the simple action of strengtheningrepeated connections and pruning neglected ones to form new concepts. Later we illustrate howprojective learning can also be used for finding causes.In the last and most central section, we outline a neural architecture for generating preference-based actions through a few tunable weights.

title: NCCL-BOT: Closing the Loop on NCCL's Cost Model with Online Bandits
abstract: NCCL picks an algorithm-protocol pair for every collective from an analytic cost model (AUTO) that never sees a measured latency. The model is a strong prior but a brittle final decision: priced on forced-arm runs, its choice is exact on most contexts and badly wrong in a few. We built NCCL-BOT, a tuner plugin that closes the loop: a per-context bandit, warm-started from the model, learns from measured latencies. We replay a forced-arm H100 sweep, tuned at 4-8 nodes and scored at 16-32, and price the model's choice on the same forced arms; that sweep has no stock-NCCL run. The bandit cuts the contexts where the model's choice loses more than 10% from 19 to 1 (p99 103% to 9.9%, mean 6.1% to 1.6%; p=0.047 over nine scenarios after Holm correction). The prior and continued learning both matter: cold-started bandits, and committing after one probe of each arm, lose more on the mean in every scenario. Supervised selectors fit once on the same data and tuned with the same budget match the mean, and their heavier tail is not significant (7 against 1 contexts above 10%, p=0.06); at seen scales they match or beat online selection. With hyperparameters frozen from H100, UCB1 cuts AUTO's p99 from 60% to 23% and from 56% to 15% on two GB200 fabrics, but its contexts above 10% go from 16 to 8 on one and from 10 to 13 on the other, and scenario-level tests do not separate the two. Live, on two latency-emulated node sets of one H100 system with one run per policy, the learners repair most of a gross AUTO error on one (selection loss 31% to 6-8% for deterministic Greedy and UCB1; average all-reduce bandwidth 1.18-1.24x stock) but average 0.94-0.99x stock on the other, and on both lose to stock below 1 MiB (on the first through plugin overhead); on H100 the cost model is exact there offline, so small sizes can be left to it. We do not show a net end-to-end win.

title: EASE-KV: Diagnosing the Gap Between Memory Availability and Effective Use
abstract: Reusable key-value (KV) memory avoids repeatedly prefilling retrieved text, but stored and injected memories do not necessarily become usable evidence. We present EASE-KV, a controlled framework for understanding this gap under fixed candidates and a frozen language model. EASE-KV separates three interfaces: whether required relations are preserved during encoding, whether preserved memories receive appropriate influence during allocation, and whether outcome supervision can identify useful allocations. Matched experiments show that causal encoding improves compositional accuracy by 25.0 percentage points over block-diagonal encoding, while the tested inference-time bridging methods fail to recover the lost contextual information. With unchanged stored states, diagnostic evidence-guided allocation improves LongMemEval accuracy from 31.2% to 38.4%, demonstrating that memory influence can be controlled without re-encoding. However, controllability does not guarantee learnability: binary correctness provides informative reward contrast for 53.0% of sampled query groups, compared with 73.6% under the evaluated shaped-reward setting. These findings show that effective KV memory requires more than retrieval and injection: the required relations must be encoded, preserved memories must receive appropriate influence, and supervision must distinguish better allocations from worse ones.

title: Single-Radar Bilateral 3D Near-Field Imaging for Mobile Robots
abstract: Mobile robots operating in homes need reliable 3D perception of nearby furniture and surrounding structures, yet recovering this information on both sides of the robot's path with a single forward-mounted millimeter-wave radar remains challenging because of near-field wavefront curvature, viewpoint-dependent target visibility, and limited elevation diversity. This paper presents a motion-assisted framework for reconstructing structures on both sides of a robot's trajectory. Our near-field model relates scene reflectivity to stepped-frequency multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) observations across frequencies and robot positions using spherical paths from transmitter (Tx) to scatterer to receiver (Rx). Bilateral Tx combining provides wideband directional weighting, while sliding-aperture back-projection coherently focuses the measurements using near-field propagation distances. Top-K power fusion combines local images with different visibility. The reconstruction provides lateral-forward support for multi-layer height extraction, followed by guarded adaptive height refinement using the original MIMO channels. Experiments in controlled, office/study, and corridor environments produce mean lateral-forward localization errors of 4.65, 5.63, and 5.98 cm, respectively, with peak-to-background ratios (PBRs) exceeding 13 dB. The framework recovers bilateral 3D scattering structure from one forward pass using a single radar, without relying on learned representations of the scene.

title: The matchgate even/odd split, kernel-checked: amplitudes are even-dimensional Pfaffians
abstract: Matchgates are classically simulable because their amplitudes are Pfaffians (signed sums over perfect matchings, equivalently square roots of determinants), and a determinant is a polynomial in its entries, computable in polynomial time. We kernel-check in Lean 4 + Mathlib the seed of that correspondence, over the complex numbers: (1) pfaffian2_sq_eq_det, the 2x2 Pfaffian (the single perfect-matching weight) squares to the determinant, so a matchgate amplitude is a Pfaffian, hence a polynomial, hence classically simulable; and (2) det_three_antisymm_eq_zero, a 3x3 antisymmetric matrix has determinant 0, so odd dimension kills the determinant and the Pfaffian (hence matchgates) is an even-dimensional object. Together these are the even/odd split behind matchgate simulability. We state honestly what is not proved: the 4x4 exact four-qubit amplitude is the next rung and is not claimed, and the full matchgate/free-fermion correspondence is the known Valiant / Jozsa-Miyake theorem, formalized here only in its seed.

title: Multi-Node Transformers for Object Detection and Captioning Across Distributed Edge Networks
abstract: This paper presents a unified transformer-based framework for object detection and dense region captioning across distributed edge networks. The architecture uses a shared visual encoder followed by detection, region extraction, and autoregressive language-decoding stages, allowing localization and region description to reuse the same image features. This design removes the second image-encoding path required by decoupled detection and captioning pipelines. To support execution on resource-limited devices, a workload-allocation formulation assigns model stages and input streams across connected edge nodes while accounting for execution time, memory capacity, processor utilization, power limits, and intermediate tensor transfer cost. The framework is evaluated on a six-device edge testbed comprising four NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and Orin NX inference nodes and two Raspberry Pi 5 auxiliary CPU nodes, with TensorRT FP16 and INT8 execution on the NVIDIA devices. On a Jetson Orin Nano, the unified INT8 model achieves 38.1 FPS with 3.5 GB peak memory use and 11.8 W measured power. Under four concurrent streams, the proposed allocation achieves 35.2 FPS and 28.4 ms mean end-to-end latency with an internode transfer rate of 6.8 MB/s.
